articles.title: House Dems plot Trump investigation blitz if they seize majority
articles.summary: Rep. Robert Garcia outlined key targets, including the Trump family, Jeffrey Epstein and ICE, as House Democrats prepare oversight investigations.
articles.body: House Democrats are planning for a slew of investigations targeting President Donald Trump, his Cabinet, and his family if they win the midterm elections. In just two months, voters across the country will decide which party controls Congress for the second half of President Donald Trump's final term. Historical trends dictate that the party in power in the White House — in this case, Republicans — usually loses one or both chambers. Democrats in the House of Representatives are already planning for that eventuality, key left-wing leaders told Fox News Digital. SEN CHUCK SCHUMER UNVEILS ANTI-CORRUPTION AGENCY AIMED AT TRUMP AND FUTURE PRESIDENTS "I'm going to start on the Department of Defense. Our service members are being put at tremendous risk. There is corruption, there's incompetence, there is nepotism at the DoD," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., told Fox News Digital. "There are very disturbing reports about ties between defense money and appropriations programs, and requests by the White House to funnel defense spending to certain companies linked to the Trump family. So we're going to take a hard look at all of that." 2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN Crow sits on the House Armed Services and Intelligence committees, in addition to co-chairing the House Anti-Corruption Caucus. He was also notably one of the impeachment managers who helped lead one of two pushes by Democrats to keep Trump out of power. Asked if impeachment could pop up again — whether for Trump or his appointees — Crow did not rule it out. GOP LAWMAKER UNVEILS HISTORIC MOVE TO 'EXPUNGE' BOTH 'MALICIOUSLY FALSE' IMPEACHMENTS AGAINST TRUMP "It's one of several tools that Congress has to pursue accountability, to get information, and to attack corruption," Crow said. "I won't hesitate to use that tool if that's the right one. But there are other tools available to us, too." Several impeachment resolutions have been introduced over the last two years targeting both Trump and his officials, but none have gained steam within the wider Democratic Caucus. HOUSE DEMS UNVEIL BILL TO EXAMINE REMOVING TRUMP USING 25TH AMENDMENT House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has demurred on multiple occasions when asked about impeachment. And it likely won't be the first tool in Democrats' arsenal that they'd wield if they win in November, two of their presumptive chairmen suggested. The most likely first approach will be tackling what Democrats see as corruption and mismanagement of federal agencies. JEFFRIES' REPORTED MEETING WITH KUSHNER ABOUT POSSIBLE TRUMP COOPERATION DRAWS LEFT-WING BACKLASH Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is poised to take over the House Oversight Committee if the chamber flips, told reporters he was already working closely with presumptive House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jamie Raskin, D-Md., on potential investigations. Garcia told Fox News Digital there were "a few key investigations" he was already looking at. MISSOURI HIGH COURT BLOCKS GOP-BACKED CONGRESSIONAL MAPS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS; TRUMP BLASTS 'RIDICULOUS' RULING "One is going to be the Trump family corruption. The second will be the Jeffrey Epstein investigation. Third will be ICE and DHS and the corruption happening there," Garcia said. "We'll also go into anyone that's ripping off the American public from a corporate perspective or CEO perspective. And then lastly, there's a lot of interest in the committee on taking on what's happening to the destruction of our vaccination process and [Health and Human Services Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr.]." Raskin, meanwhile, has already previewed what his panel's investigations would look like. He's sent a flurry of requests for information targeting the business dealings of Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, as well as Donald Trump Jr. and FBI Director Kash Patel, among others. TODD BLANCHE SAYS 'NO CLOSED INVESTIGATIONS' IN EPSTEIN CASE, VOWS DOJ WILL PURSUE NEW SUSPECTS "The Trump family has turned the entire executive branch into a money-making enterprise, so there’s more than enough corruption and lawlessness to keep Democrats across the House busy for years. Judiciary Democrats are already following the evidence wherever it leads, from the Trump family’s astonishing self-dealing and conflicts of interest to the corporations and law firms that have colluded with this administration for profit, advantage and protection," Raskin told Fox News Digital when asked about his plans. "We will continue to work together across committees and use every investigative and legislative tool we have to uncover the facts, expose the wrongdoing and its costs for the public, hold the perpetrators and profiteers accountable, and pass legislative cures." Republicans have long feared that Democrats winning either the House or Senate will grind the GOP's agenda to a halt in Washington. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., previously told Fox News Digital that he believed Democrats would try to impeach Trump "on Day 1" if they win. Trump, meanwhile, has maintained his innocence amid an array of accusations from the left. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: MIKE DAVIS: Trump's ballroom win highlights need for serious judicial nominees
articles.summary: The Supreme Court's 5-4 ruling on the White House ballroom lawsuit exposes deep rifts, with Chief Justice John Roberts penning a sharp dissent.
articles.body: Last year, President Trump ordered construction of a White House ballroom and a secure underground military facility. A DC busybody sued to stop it, and on Aug. 31, the Supreme Court killed this laughable lawsuit by a single vote. Mid-construction, long after the East Wing’s demolition, Chief Justice John Roberts joined the three Democrat women to try to shut down the president of the United States’ security improvement, expressly permitted by federal statute and Article II of the Constitution, to the White House complex. This narrow 5-4 ruling proves precisely why Republicans must continue to nominate and confirm rock-solid constitutionalists all across the federal judiciary. For decades, the White House hosted large events in outdoor tents, with women’s high heels sinking into the soggy Rose Garden and other White House grounds. But that open setting provides a rich target for terrorists, including too many of today’s Democrats, who wish to harm the president. The threat is all too real. Just over two years ago, Matthew Thomas Crooks nearly assassinated Trump at an open-air campaign rally in Butler, Pa. Two months later, Ryan Routh attempted another assassination of Trump at a Florida golf course. In April, a third would-be assassin attempted to murder Trump in a DC hotel ballroom at the annual White House Correspondents’ Dinner. The dire need for a highly secure White House ballroom is obvious—and presidents and their guests long after Trump will enjoy its beauty, utility, and convenience. The White House regularly hosts heads of state, members of Congress, foreign diplomats, and other high-value targets of America’s enemies. Any reasonable person ought to know that, in these disturbing times, we need the most enhanced security imaginable. Trump acted. He ordered the demolition of the run-down, long-past-its-prime White House East Wing to build a privately funded, 70-foot-tall indoor ballroom, a subterranean military bunker, and rooftop security facility. WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS' DINNER SHOOTING SHARPENS FOCUS ON TRUMP’S BALLROOM CONSTRUCTION PROPOSAL Enter Alison Hoagland, an underworked DC busybody and member of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, who claims she leisurely strolls by the White House vicinity about once a month —while real Americans, in real America, work real jobs. She filed suit, claiming the new ballroom was unsightly and offended her apparently very delicate aesthetic sensibilities. DC U.S. District Judge Richard Leon, a George W. Bush appointee who suffers from severe Trump Derangement Syndrome like so many other Republican-appointed DC federal judges, took the bait. He blocked all new above-ground construction for the East Wing unless the subsurface military facility strictly required it. APPEALS COURT LETS TRUMP RESUME WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM CONSTRUCTION, SEEKS LOWER COURT CLARITY DC federal judges are legendary for their self-imagined expertise in . . . well, everything. But a judge who has never had a real job in his adult life deluding himself into believing his job is now to moonlight as the construction foreman over the White House complex, instead of the duly-elected president of the United States (who happens to be one of the best builders in the world for over 50 years), is next-level judicial narcissism and lawlessness. Unsurprisingly, the Democrat-dominated DC Circuit upheld Leon’s rogue ruling over a superb dissent by U.S. Circuit Judge Neomi Rao, a former law clerk to America’s all-time-greatest Justice Clarence Thomas. The Trump administration took the fight to the Supreme Court, as these DC federal courts would turn the White House complex into a stop-work construction site for years. TRUMP'S WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM CONSTRUCTION GETS ANOTHER LIFELINE FROM SCOTUS AMID HEATED LEGAL FIGHT Article III of the U.S. Constitution requires a plaintiff to have standing. In order to bring suit in federal court, a plaintiff needs a concrete, redressable injury that has already occurred or which imminently looms. articles.title: Hunter Biden: ‘I may have to’ run for president in 2028
articles.summary: Former President Biden’s (D) son, Hunter Biden, said that he may have to consider a 2028 presidential run amid speculation on who the Democratic nominee could be. In a conversation with radio host John Catsimatidis, Biden was asked if had any plans to run for president where he said, “If I get your [Catsimatidis] endorsement,…
articles.body:
Former President Biden’s (D) son, Hunter Biden, said that he may have to consider a 2028 presidential run amid speculation on who the Democratic nominee could be.

In a conversation with radio host John Catsimatidis, Biden was asked if had any plans to run for president where he said, “If I get your [Catsimatidis] endorsement, I may have to.”

When asked the same question earlier Biden stated, “I haven’t made up my mind.”

“The truth of the matter is that I think we have an incredible bench,” he said on “The Cats Roundtable,” mentioning Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) and Illinois Governor JB Pritzker (D) before declaring “I love Gavin Newsom, personally.”

The governor of the nation’s most populous state has been open about his interest in seeking the top office. Newsom said in October 2025 that he would be “lying” if he said he wasn’t considering a bid for the White House after the 2026 midterms.

Other potential contenders include Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), former Vice President Kamala Harris and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

Biden expressed during this interview that no matter who the candidate was, he wanted, “the next president to commit to one thing: to commit to adhering to the rule of law. To commit to the idea that we believe in this constitutional republic and the aspirations of normal Americans.”

“I truly, truly want whoever is our president to succeed. But particularly succeed in keeping this country safe. That’s their primary responsibility,” he said.

An Emerson College and The Hill survey that ranked potential match-ups between potential GOP and Democratic presidential candidates found Biden’s pick in a decent position.

Newsom held small leads over both potential Republican nominees, Vice President J.D. Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, unlike Ocasio-Cortez, who trailed both candidates.

Biden added that what he cared about right now “is the 50 million Americans that are still suffering sick … with their addictions.”

While acknowledging his struggles with substance abuse issues, he noted in the interview that he recently celebrated seven and a half years of sobriety.

articles.title: Dems descend on posh island getaway packed with deep-pocketed donors as midterms close in
articles.summary: Hakeem Jeffries, Jon Ossoff and Josh Turek are among Democrats flocking to Nantucket to court wealthy donors despite the party's anti-elite rhetoric.
articles.body: Democrats have made summer pilgrimages to Nantucket, tapping the wealthy Massachusetts island’s donor class as candidates and party leaders stockpile campaign cash ahead of November. Nantucket and neighboring Martha’s Vineyard have long been magnets for political fundraising, and Democrats are again tapping the islands’ deep-pocketed donor networks as candidates and party leaders build their war chests ahead of November’s midterm elections. As of June 30, the Democratic National Committee, Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee had about $136 million in combined cash on hand, compared with roughly $277 million held by their Republican counterparts, according to federal filings. This summer, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Texas Senate candidate James Talarico, Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., and others have been spotted on the island for fundraising events. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: AS DEMOCRATS TURN LEFT, BLACK VOTERS TAP THE BRAKES Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., reportedly went to Nantucket for an Aug. 29 fundraiser hosted by Democratic heavyweight Elizabeth Frawley Bagley, a Biden-appointed U.S. ambassador to Brazil who served as ambassador to Portugal under President Bill Clinton, according to the Boston Globe. The Democratic fundraising circuit extends to neighboring Martha's Vineyard, another exclusive Massachusetts vacation destination. Former President Barack Obama visited Martha's Vineyard on Aug. 31 for an event hosted by former Attorney General Eric Holder benefiting the National Democratic Redistricting Committee. Wes Moore, a possible 2028 presidential contender, was on Martha’s Vineyard the weekend of Aug. 8 for a DNC fundraiser with DNC Chair Ken Martin. "Where was Wes Moore last weekend? Not campaigning in Maryland or solving our problems in Annapolis, but speaking at a national Democrat event in Martha’s Vineyard. Wes Moore's priority isn’t Maryland, and it will never be Maryland. His only focus is growing his national profile and running for President in 2028. Elect Dan Cox for a Governor who will put Maryland and the needs of Marylanders first," wrote Maryland GOP at the time. Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek, a Democratic nominee for the open Senate seat held by retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst, was spotted on Nantucket while the Iowa State Fair was still underway. Turek, who had appeared at the fair earlier in the week, did not answer a reporter’s questions about his fundraising stop, according to videos on social media. Democratic donors Frank Herron and Sandra Urie, who hosted first lady Jill Biden for a 2022 Democratic National Committee fundraiser at their Nantucket home, hosted Moulton for a Nantucket fundraising brunch on Aug. 2, according to local paper Nantucket Current. JON OSSOFF DODGES ON WHY HE INVOKED TRUMP AIDE'S NAME DURING GEORGIA CAMPAIGN RALLY Michelle Obama was also on the island, on Aug. 23, but was there to promote her book, "The Look," at two sold-out conversations at the Performing Arts Center in Oak Bluffs. The Obamas have had a vacation house on the Vineyard since 2019. Nantucket has long been a destination for prominent Democrats as well as celebrities, millionaires and billionaires. Former President Joe Biden and his family have traveled to the island for decades to celebrate Thanksgiving. Former first lady Jill Biden was also spotted on the island in July to promote her new book, "View From the East Wing: A Memoir." DEM ATTORNEY BACKS GOP HOPEFUL IN MICHIGAN RACE AGAINST EL-SAYED, 'JUMPING SHIP' FROM HIS PARTY'S 'LUNATICS' Republicans have also tapped Nantucket’s deep-pocketed donor circuit. Rick Scott and fellow Senate candidates Ted Budd, Dr. Mehmet Oz and Herschel Walker for another fundraising jaunt on the affluent island. articles.title: Kushner, Witkoff set for Kyiv talks after Putin meeting in US push for peace
articles.summary: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Vladimir Putin for over three hours in Moscow before heading to Kyiv to meet Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
articles.body: U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv on Sunday for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, a day after meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow as part of efforts to end the war between the two countries. Zelenskyy said Sunday morning that he had met with his negotiating team ahead of the Americans' arrival and that Kyiv was prepared for the discussions. "Ukraine has always been and will remain constructive," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer. Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A dignified character of the postwar peace is needed." "Our proposals are ready," he added. "It is important to work in a coordinated, substantive, and realistic manner." CIA DIRECTOR JOHN RATCLIFFE MET WITH RUSSIAN INTELLIGENCE OFFICIALS IN VISIT TO MOSCOW, KREMLIN SAYS Witkoff and Kushner met with Putin for more than three hours behind closed doors Saturday, though the talks ended without any announced breakthroughs. Putin’s foreign policy advisor Yuri Ushakov described the meeting as "constructive, frank and useful," but did not disclose specific outcomes. A White House official said following the meeting that the two sides discussed "substantive plans for next steps," which are expected to be announced in the coming weeks. The official added that the U.S. delegation looked forward to "equally productive meetings" in Ukraine. The Kyiv meeting comes as Washington seeks to revive efforts to reach a settlement in a war that began with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Those efforts had lost momentum over the past six months as U.S. attention shifted to the war with Iran. PUTIN AND IRAN 'NEED EACH OTHER DESPERATELY,' EXPERT SAYS, AS RUSSIA VOICES SUPPORT FOR REGIME Significant differences between Moscow and Kyiv remain, including over territory. Kyiv has rejected Russia’s demand that Ukraine withdraw from portions of the eastern Donetsk and Luhansk regions that remain under Ukrainian control. Ushakov said Moscow provided the U.S. delegation with its "comprehensive assessment" of the battlefield during Saturday's meeting, though the discussions extended beyond the war. "Economic issues and potentially large, mutually beneficial joint projects for Russia and America were discussed in considerable detail," Ushakov said. President Donald Trump said Friday that he dispatched Witkoff and Kushner, his son-in-law and advisor, to determine whether progress toward a peace agreement could be made. "We have an idea for peace. I sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, two great negotiators," Trump told reporters. "They've done a great job, and we sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done. And there may be a good chance that we'll do it." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The diplomatic push comes as Russia and Ukraine continue to exchange drone and missile attacks. Both sides reported strikes overnight into Sunday despite agreeing to pause attacks on each other's capitals during the negotiations. Fox News Digital’s Robert McGreevy and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump is waging a war on America’s children — and he’s winning
articles.summary: “Children are the world’s most valuable resource,” John F. Kennedy proclaimed, “and its best hope for the future.” Apparently, the Trump administration does not agree.
articles.body:
President Trump’s administration is waging war against children, especially those in our nation’s poorest families. Here are a few of the fronts on which that undeclared war is being fought, with devastating consequences for the next generation of Americans.

Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act made massive cuts to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program or SNAP, leaving millions of children in low-income families without access to health insurance, adequate and healthy food and, in some cases, learning and developmental services in public schools.

Roughly 40 percent of American children receive health coverage through Medicaid. Although the bill’s work requirements do not apply to children, they lose coverage when their parents do. The Congressional Budget Office estimates the cuts will increase the number of Americans without health insurance by 7.5 million in 2034.

The budget office also projects that SNAP spending will decline by $211 billion through 2035. An analysis by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates 1.5 million children, conservatively, have lost benefits since July 2025. Further reductions are likely as states are forced to pay a larger share of the program’s administrative costs.

The 2025 bill did increase the Child Tax Credit from $2,000 to $2,200. But it left intact rules that prevent many low-income families from receiving the full credit. As a result, 30 percent of all children and 99 percent of those from the poorest one-fifth of families won’t benefit from the increase.

Each of these individual policies is onerous, but the collective impact is especially damaging, since many families will be hurt by all of them.

The Trump administration’s vaccine policies have put children at risk as well. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his handpicked appointees have promoted vaccine skepticism , parental choice and limits to state requirements that children be vaccinated before they start school. They claim, without evidence, that COVID-19 vaccines have killed children and that vaccines cause autism .

As a result, vaccination rates are falling. The share of kindergartners exempted from one or more required vaccines has increased from 2.2 percent in 2020-2021 to 4.2 percent in 2025. Only 92 percent of kindergarten students now get the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, well below the 95 percent needed for herd immunity.

The consequences are not hypothetical. Americans have experienced the largest measles outbreak in three decades, with the vast majority of cases among unvaccinated children.

Yet Trump’s Aug. 10 executive order pares back the number of recommended childhood vaccines and calls for splitting the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three separately administered shots — changes strongly opposed by mainstream medical organizations because they will leave many more children vulnerable to preventable diseases.

That same month, the Trump administration proposed deregulating Head Start, one of the country’s most important programs for poor children. Head Start provides preschool, child care, meals and support services to about 700,000 children , many of them homeless, in foster care or disabled. The administration has already closed half of Head Start’s regional offices . Now it intends to reduce the federal overhead payments from 15 percent to 5 percent and eliminate or dilute national standards governing student-teacher ratios, educational requirements, medical screenings, program hours and other services.

The administration claims these changes will reduce costs and allow Head Start to serve more children. But this approach removes requirements intended to bolster program quality. Project 2025, it is worth noting, advocated eliminating Head Start . The administration’s approach will, at a minimum, dramatically reduce its effectiveness.

Meanwhile, tens of thousands of children whose parents have been arrested, detained or deported, or fear they will be, are suffering serious and lasting effects. Faced with economic instability, loss of housing, absence from school, fewer doctor visits, and sometimes foster care, they experience separation anxiety , headaches, stomach aches, difficulty sleeping and eating, and anxiety and depression.

More than 12,000 children and their parents or sponsors have been arrested following tips from the federal Office of Refugee Resettlement, an office that previously maintained a sharp separation between child-welfare responsibilities and immigration enforcement so parents would not be prevented from reuniting with their children.

Trump’s war on children doesn’t stop at America’s borders. Researchers estimate that reductions in health care, nutrition, clean water and sanitation caused by the evisceration of USAID will lead to the deaths of about 4.5 million children under the age of five by 2030.

The administration insists its policies will reduce wasteful spending, encourage work, promote parental rights, enforce immigration laws and return authority to the states. But wars are — and should be — measured by their casualties. Across an extraordinary range of administration policies, children, who are least able to protect themselves, are “collateral damage.”

“Children are the world’s most valuable resource,” President John F. Kennedy proclaimed , “and its best hope for the future.” Apparently, the Trump administration does not agree.

David Wippman is emeritus president of Hamilton College. Glenn C. Altschuler is the Thomas and Dorothy Litwin Emeritus Professor of American Studies at Cornell University.

articles.title: ‘Destroying the American way of life’: El-Sayed’s political orbit complicates effort to moderate his image
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed claims he's not a socialist, but Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Democratic Socialists of America ties tell a different story.
articles.body: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is seeking to appear more moderate to voters while, at the same time, maintaining ties to individuals who take positions far to the left of anything he publicly endorses. Since launching his Senate bid in April 2025, El-Sayed has distanced himself from a number of positions he had previously held and scrubbed much of his left-wing pre-campaign content from the internet. He has also repeatedly insisted that he is "not a socialist." While attempting to convince voters that characterizations of him as a left-wing ideologue are inaccurate, El-Sayed has appeared at campaign events with and accepted endorsements from a range of political allies and supporters with controversial records or views. EL-SAYED’S HASAN PIKER PROBLEM FOLLOWS HIM TO DEM CONVENTION AS JEWISH VOTERS BREAK RANKS Beyond campaigning with Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who claimed that America "deserved" 9/11, El-Sayed has also linked himself with terror-sympathetic Islamic clerics, individuals accused of antisemitism and several prominent socialists and socialist-aligned activists. El-Sayed's campaign has attempted to flip the narrative on Republicans, pointing out that Mike Rogers, the GOP nominee facing off against him, has his own set of controversial associations. Some individuals affiliated with the Rogers campaign, which did not respond to a request for comment, have also cast doubt on the outcome of the 2020 election and advocated for banning gay marriage. Nonetheless, Republicans have made El-Sayed's affiliations with controversial figures a focal point of their campaign in Michigan. Surrounded by socialists "I am not somebody who is a socialist," El-Sayed told CNN in July. "I believe in capitalism, I just believe that capitalism has to be regulated." Despite this assertion, and multiple others like it, El-Sayed has surrounded himself with socialists during his tenure as a public figure. Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont described by some as the avatar of socialism in America, threw his support behind El-Sayed’s ill-fated 2018 gubernatorial run. The Vermont socialist was also among the first to back El-Sayed’s 2026 Senate bid, endorsing him on the same day he launched his campaign. Sanders isn’t the only socialist backing El-Sayed’s run for Senate. Reps. Rashida Tlaib, Summer Lee and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez are all vocal supporters. TOP DEM HOPEFUL FLIPS SCRIPT AFTER YEARS IN SOCIALIST ORBIT WITH PUZZLING CLAIM El-Sayed has long aligned himself with the Democratic Socialists of America, only recently distancing himself from the ascendant left-wing organization as he seeks to win a competitive Senate race. Between 2017 and 2020, the Michigan Democrat spoke at six events held by Democratic Socialists of America chapters, including a 2019 fundraiser where he served as the keynote speaker. Additionally, DSA officials told Politico in July that they were mobilizing resources to help El-Sayed win his Democratic primary election. "I'm not technically or practically DSA," El-Sayed told the Wall Street Journal in July. Socialist organizers, however, have called him "a longtime friend of Detroit DSA." Most recently, news broke that William Lawrence, a Democratic Socialists of America member running for Congress in Michigan who has campaigned alongside El-Sayed, called for "destroying the American way of life" on a podcast hosted by Marxist activists. "I'm wondering how we can inspire a sense of abundance for people in the United States, while frankly, destroying the American way of life and the negative connotations and material realities that has come to mean," he said on the episode. 'Martyrs' and 'mujahideen' A strong showing with Michigan’s Arab American community helped carry El-Sayed to victory in August’s Democratic primary. El-Sayed has been deeply involved with the state’s Muslim community, including relationships with figures who have made controversial statements about Israel, Hamas and Hezbollah. ‘MARTYRS’: MICHIGAN DEMS NOMINATE HEZBOLLAH-PRAISING CANDIDATE AFTER OUSTING JEWISH REGENT In April, Amir Makled, a man running for the University of Michigan's board of regents who celebrated dead members of Hezbollah — a U.S.-designated terrorist organization — as "martyr[s]," introduced El-Sayed at a campaign rally. Then, in June, El-Sayed headlined the opening of Imam Hassan Qazwini’s Islamic Institute of America, offering him his "hearty congratulations" and calling his mosque "incredible." Qazwini has a history of making controversial comments. Among these have been his claim that Israel was behind ISIS, calling a slain leader of Hezbollah a hero of the "resistance," and describing Sanders as honorable "even though he is a Jew." Sanders’ 2020 presidential campaign denounced Qazwini as antisemitic. Qazwini has since compelled his congregation to vote for El-Sayed, arguing that doing so is a "moral responsibility" and "religious duty" in a July sermon. At the opening of Qazwini’s institute, El-Sayed shared the stage with Sheikh Fadhel al-Sahlani, a cleric who praised Hamas’ Oct. 7 terrorist attack and downplayed the number of people killed in the Holocaust. EL-SAYED BOOKED FOR MAJOR ISLAMIC CONVENTION ALONGSIDE CLERICS WITH RADICAL PASTS On Sept. 5, El-Sayed is scheduled to share a different stage at the Islamic Society of North America’s annual convention with Qazwini. Also slated to be in attendance are Imam Baqir Berry, who prayed that God would grant Islamic holy soldiers in Gaza "a mighty victory;" and Siraj Wahhaj, who was named as a possible co-conspirator in the 1993 World Trade Center terrorism case but was never charged in connection with the attacks. El-Sayed’s religious views have puzzled some observers. While the Democrat supports easy access to abortion and child sex changes, he has also expressed a desire to live in accordance with Sharia law and describes his faith as important to his outlook on life. Ties to Nation of Islam figures A number of people El-Sayed has appeared with or promoted have ties to the Nation of Islam, a religious organization founded by Black nationalists in the 1930s that is not considered an orthodox Muslim sect by most Islamic leaders. The Nation of Islam teaches that Black people are the original human beings and that White people were created by an evil Black scientist named Yakub. Their doctrine portrays the White race as inherently corrupt and historically responsible for oppressing Black people, though it also asserts Black racial superiority. Currently, the Nation of Islam is under the leadership of Louis Farrakhan. Farrakhan has accused Jews of being "wicked deceivers of the American people" who have "sucked their blood," later suggesting that "people will never be free in this country" until they are liberated from the "tremendous amount of influence" he said Jews exert over the American government. He has also called Jews "termites" and suggested that White people generally are "the skunk of the planet earth" and not fully evolved. EL-SAYED TOUTS ENDORSEMENT FROM PASTOR WHO PRAISED NOTORIOUS ANTISEMITE INFAMOUS FOR CALLING JEWS ‘TERMITES’ Despite the Nation of Islam’s controversial positions, El-Sayed has maintained ties to individuals affiliated with it. The leader of the Detroit chapter of the Nation of Islam, meanwhile, posted a picture of him and El-Sayed shaking hands at a 2025 NAACP event. articles.title: As Trump pushes for data centers, voters in key midterm races say they don’t want them
articles.summary: An NBC News Decision Desk Poll found that that 69% of respondents oppose the construction of AI data centers in their local area, with 45% saying they “strongly oppose” the idea.
articles.body: DES MOINES, Iowa — Dawn Vogel, a Republican county supervisor in rural Buchanan County, Iowa, doesn’t have a lot in common with the leading democratic socialists in Congress. But on this bit of policy they agree: Data centers are proliferating across the American landscape too fast. Vogel voted earlier this year for a moratorium that temporarily bans data centers from setting up shop in her heavily Republican county, which favored President Donald Trump 63%-35% in 2024. In Washington, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. — the nation’s two most prominent democratic socialists — have proposed a similar moratorium that would cover the entire country. “I don’t think this is a Republican or Democratic issue,” Vogel said on the sidelines of the Iowa State Association of Counties’ annual conference here in late August, adding that she hasn’t talked to a single voter at home who wants data centers. “It’s an issue of what’s the best use for the land, what’s the best use for our natural resources,” she said. “You can have all the data you want to in the world, but if you don’t have water to drink, you don’t have humans to use the data.” That point of view places Vogel in a loose, but very large, populist coalition that is fighting the rise of data centers at the ballot box, with yard signs, in courts and at all levels of government as November’s midterm elections approach. An NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey, conducted from Aug. 20 through Sept. 1, found that 69% of respondents oppose the construction of AI data centers in their local area, with 45% saying they “strongly oppose” the idea. They are all at odds with President Donald Trump. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post at the end of August. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.” But it’s more about backyards than being seen as backward, according to voters who spoke to NBC News on a recent road trip along Interstate 80 from Nebraska to New Jersey — a swath that includes eight swing districts key to determining which party will control the House next year and two marquee Senate races. These voters, who span the political spectrum, said they don’t want data centers anywhere near their communities. For some, the issue has become a touchstone for the feeling that the powerful are taking advantage of the powerless. “All of the data centers that are starting to pop up in areas, I find that troublesome because it drives utility costs for citizens in the area,” said Tamara Clark, 49, a Democratic voter who works in the healthcare industry. “I don’t feel like the rich should continuously get rich while we have to grovel for what we need in our everyday necessities.” In Clark’s congressional district, Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, a 22-term incumbent, is using the issue against her rival, Republican Derek Merrin, who cast a 2017 vote in the state Legislature that helped extend tax breaks to companies that build data centers in the state. Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who is seeking to hold his seat against Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown, was a full-throated advocate for data centers when he was the state’s lieutenant governor. But in July, he introduced legislation in the Senate that would require utility companies to charge large-scale data center operators enough money to cover the costs of increased electricity and water use. His change of tune reflects a broader shift among elected officials who embraced data centers as a way to bring jobs and tax revenue to their cities, counties and states. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, D-Pa., who is on the ballot in November, signed a new batch of data center regulations in August after having encouraged companies to locate them in his state. While Republican voters are more supportive of data centers than Democrats and independents, the majority of them remain opposed — 57% to 43% — according to the NBC News Decision Desk poll. The survey found that 81% of Democrats and 71% of independents are against data centers being built in their communities. While supporters have been less demonstrative, their ranks extend beyond the AI companies building data centers and the politicians who have looked to them as economic development engines. National and local labor unions involved in the construction and maintenance of data centers tout them as a boon for workers, both as a source of jobs and for high rates of pay. Several data center workers in Ohio spoke to NBC News about those benefits on the condition of anonymity because, according to one of them, they have agreed not to discuss their jobs with the media. That worker said he can make as much as $5,000 in a week, including overtime, at a relatively low-level union job. “It’s helping a lot of people — a lot of work going on, a lot of people benefiting from it,” the data center worker said, adding that he was warned by friends about problems, from overuse of water resources to weird ringing sounds, that he has not witnessed at his workplace. “It’s scary,” he said. “You got a lot of people that say all these horrific things. I was told all these negative things about data centers, and then I started working at one, and I didn’t see any of the things I was told about.” He said he would like to see proponents and critics work together to fix any problems with data centers so that they can continue to be built and operate without disruption to the surrounding communities. But Jordan Cloe, 47, an electrician from Bondurant, in Iowa’s hotly contested 3rd Congressional District, said he’s worried about the resources used by a data center in neighboring Altoona. “Did we have any data on what the implications were about water consumption or anything? Like, we just built a power grid where that thing sits,” he said. “Did we get to use that? No, they gobbled that up.” Cloe, who said he aligns more with Democrats, said he doesn’t know anything about Sarah Trone Garriott, the Democratic challenger to Republican Rep. Zach Nunn, but that he plans to vote for her in November. For Vogel, the county supervisor, the unresolved questions are enough reason to keep data centers out of her county — at least for now. “We need to do what’s best for Buchanan County and then, you know, if the companies want to come knock on the door,” she said, “then we’ll talk.”

articles.title: Trump's approval drops among Republicans ahead of midterms, new poll shows
articles.summary: NBC News unveiled new polling that shows a drop in approval for President Donald Trump among Republicans.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's support among Republican voters dropped in a new poll less than two months from November's crucial midterm elections.

An NBC News Decision Desk survey conducted from Aug. 20 to Sept. 1 found a near 10 percentage point drop among Republicans who say they "strongly approve" of the president's job performance. In polling conducted in March and April, 52% of Republicans said they strongly approved of the president's performance, compared to 31% who said they somewhat approve. Now, 41% of Republicans said they strongly approve, and those who somewhat approve have jumped to 39%.

The results, unveiled by the network's star data expert Steve Kornacki, found that Trump's overall approval rating landed at 36% – marking a record NBC polling low this term. That's also close to a low of 33% in a Reuters poll released last month .

The polling comes as Americans brace for the final quarter of the year amid economic fears and growing uncertainty about the Iran war .

articles.title: Letitia James’ Times Square shooting probe draws GOP criticism over New York’s mental health crisis
articles.summary: Saritha Komatireddy proposes a new Office of Civil Commitment after the Times Square fatal stabbing, saying New York fails mentally ill people.
articles.body: New York Attorney General Letitia James is facing scrutiny after opening up a legally required investigation into the police shooting of a woman who fatally stabbed Erin Piacenti, Bank of America executive and a new mother in her first week back to work from maternity leave, in Times Square. James' office announced on Wednesday that it will be investigating Pamela Cisneros' death, who was wielding two large knives in each hand when officers confronted her following the fatal stabbing. She was ordered to drop the weapons but did not comply and was shot when she moved toward the officers. Under state law, the Attorney General's Office of Special Investigation is mandated to investigate all deaths that were caused by police officers. However, Republican attorney general candidate Saritha Komatireddy is pushing the Attorney General's Office to take more concrete steps to ensure that another tragic killing or attack caused by a mentally unstable person doesn't happen again. She argued that an investigation into police conduct fails to address the real problem. "The problem is that we have people who are known dangerous individuals, people with documented mental illness," Komatireddy told Fox News Digital. "They've been in the courts before, or they've been to the hospitals before. The police know exactly who they are, but we have no ability to take care of them." REPUBLICANS GET 'AGGRESSIVE' IN FIGHT TO WIN TOP COP SPOTS IN BATTLEGROUND STATES A campaign spokesperson for James accused Komatireddy of seeking to "score cheap political points off of a tragedy." "Saritha Komatireddy wants to be Attorney General but doesn’t understand the law," a spokesperson said in an email to Fox News Digital. "Under New York’s Executive Law, the Office of the Attorney General’s Office of Special Investigation is required to investigate any incident where a police officer’s actions may have caused a death, including this one." However, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has a history of anti-police rhetoric, applauded the officers who stopped Cisneros. "I want to thank the NYPD officers who stepped in and prevented a horrific attack from becoming even worse," Mamdani said at a news conference. PARENTS IN BRONX NEIGHBORHOOD PLEAD FOR NYPD GUARD AS MAMDANI CUTS COPS, HALTS HIRES: 'HORRIBLE SITUATION' New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch shared that while Cisneros, who lived in Queens, didn't have an arrest record in the city, there were two times police responded to calls concerning her suffering a mental health crisis. In March 2019, Cisneros attempted suicide by jumping onto the tracks of the E train and was removed and later hospitalized. In March 2018, police found her in Midtown, where she was screaming, acting belligerent and intoxicated. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255). Under the state's Mental Hygiene Law, police and doctors can take a person to the hospital for a psychological hold if they are deemed to be a risk to themselves or others, or they can not meet their basic needs — but often times those with severe mental illnesses are released by the hospital back onto the streets hours after being brought in. LETITIA JAMES FACES SCRUTINY AFTER NEW YORK CITY SPENDS $81,700 PER HOMELESS PERSON AMID SHELTER SCANDALS "I was there in Times Square — just a couple of days after this fatal stabbing — and I was walking around and saw severely mentally ill people on the street," Komatireddy told Fox News Digital. "It's still happening every day, and we need someone who's actually going to propose a real solution and way forward." TRUMP WANTS TO HELP 146,000 MENTALLY ILL WHO ARE HOMELESS. DEMOCRATS WANT TO STOP HIM The New York State Office of Mental Health is tasked with overseeing the state's mental health system, which includes 23 psychiatric centers and 6,500 programs overseen by local governments and nonprofits. In addition, Komatireddy said that, if elected, she'd create a new office known as the Office of Civil Commitment that would target and keep tabs on people who are at most risk. "The Office of Civil Commitment that I'm going to launch will be staffed with both law enforcement personnel and also physicians, and you need both because, under state law, the law requires that physicians certify that someone has the mental state required for involuntary civil commitment," Komatireddy told Fox News Digital. "So there's nothing like that right now in New York state. There's no office that has both law enforcement and physicians who can work together to get these people off the streets." Greene County Sheriff Peter Kusminsky told Fox News Digital that his deputies are not trained to handle psychiatric crises — and that the county has nowhere to send people who need real care. Deputies are constantly pulled off patrol for mental-health calls, he said, then left to put those in crisis in hotels because there aren't enough hospital beds available. "Additionally, we really struggle when we have people in custody who we aren't equipped to handle, and secure beds are even harder to find," Kusminsky said. "It sometimes takes weeks or months to locate once and when we do, they are maybe on the other side of the state and at an exorbitant cost." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Hotels and motels don’t have doctors, don’t have medicine, don’t have therapy," Komatireddy said. "The state needs to step in."

articles.title: 8 everyday things that would quit working without data centers
articles.summary: Data centers power everything from streaming and gaming to AI chatbots and fraud detection. Here's how they quietly run the apps you use daily.
articles.body: Data centers are the largely unseen infrastructure behind modern life, powering everything from the apps on your phone and shows you stream to online shopping, banking and artificial intelligence. Inside these warehouse-sized facilities, thousands of servers store data, process digital requests and keep online services running around the clock. Most Americans may never see one, but they rely on them constantly, often without realizing it. "Data centers have been around for as long as technology has been around," Brittany Kaiser, CEO of Alpha Compute, told Fox News Digital. "Anytime you’re touching technology and using everything from social media to your email, all of that information, all of the data is being processed in a data center." As more of the economy moves online, data centers have become far more than a niche piece of the tech industry. They are increasingly essential infrastructure for everyday American life. The U.S. is home to roughly 4,000 operational facilities, with thousands more planned or under construction as demand for cloud computing and AI accelerates. Here are eight ways data centers quietly power the services Americans rely on every day. 1. They make your favorite apps work From Instagram and TikTok to Gmail and banking apps, data centers process and store the information behind the services people use every day. When you open an app, upload a photo, refresh your feed or send a message, your phone is connected to servers that retrieve and deliver that information in seconds. The apps may live on a screen in your hand, but much of the work happens far away inside a physical facility filled with computers running continuously. 2. They keep your streaming and gaming smooth Netflix, YouTube, Spotify and other streaming platforms rely on massive computing infrastructure to deliver movies, videos and music to millions of users at once. Data centers help store enormous libraries of content and move it quickly enough to prevent the pauses and buffering that frustrate viewers. ONE OF AMERICA'S OLDEST MANUFACTURERS SAYS AI IS CREATING JOBS — NOT REPLACING THEM Online games also rely on data centers to connect players, synchronize what is happening in a match and reduce the lag that can make a game unplayable. The more people stream, game and use data-heavy services, the more computing power those platforms need behind the scenes. 3. They store your photos and files Your iPhone photos, Google Drive documents and cloud backups do not just float around in cyberspace. They are stored on physical servers inside data centers, often with copies kept in multiple locations to help prevent data loss. That means a lost phone or broken laptop does not necessarily mean lost memories or work file — but it also means the cloud depends on vast amounts of real-world hardware. 4. They help Google answer your questions instantly Search engines rely on data centers to sort through enormous amounts of information and return results in fractions of a second. Every query triggers systems that locate relevant webpages, images, maps, videos and other information before sending the results back to your device. What feels like a simple Google search is actually a complex exchange between your device and powerful servers processing requests at an enormous scale. 5. They make online shopping possible When you order something online, data centers help manage inventory, process payments, make product recommendations and track packages to your door. They also allow retailers to update product availability and pricing quickly as demand changes. ELECTION WHISTLEBLOWER WARNS FOREIGN ACTORS ARE SPENDING BILLIONS TO TURN AMERICANS AGAINST AI During major shopping events such as Black Friday, those systems have to handle a surge of shoppers and transactions without crashing. 6. They keep GPS and navigation running Google Maps, Waze and other navigation services depend on computing infrastructure to process traffic patterns, routes and location data in real time. They combine information from roads, users, businesses and mapping systems to estimate travel times and suggest alternate routes. Without the data centers behind them, navigation apps would not be able to react as quickly to accidents, congestion or changing road conditions. 7. They make remote work possible Video calls, cloud-based software, shared documents and workplace messaging all rely heavily on data-center infrastructure. Every Zoom meeting, Slack message and live edit to a shared file depends on servers that keep information synced between people working from different locations. THIS TINY FARMING TOWN YOU’VE NEVER HEARD OF IS HELPING MICROSOFT SELL AMERICA ON DATA CENTERS For many companies, data centers have become as essential to day-to-day operations as office space, phones and electricity. 8. They power the next generation of technology Every time someone asks an AI chatbot a question, generates an image or uses an AI-powered search feature, data centers provide the computing power working behind the screen. Those requests require far more processing than a basic web search because the systems must analyze information and generate a response in real time. That is a major reason the technology industry is racing to build bigger and more powerful data centers, often equipped with specialized chips designed for AI workloads. GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO BY CLICKING HERE In addition, autonomous vehicles, advanced robotics, scientific research and other emerging technologies require increasingly powerful computing infrastructure. Data centers help train the AI systems behind those tools, process huge volumes of data and support the software that allows them to improve over time.

articles.title: Rep. Jamie Raskin says impeachment isn’t a ‘fetish’ for Democrats but ‘a critical tool’
articles.summary: Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., that Trump has committed impeachable offenses in his second term, saying that impeachment is a “critical tool” for Democrats but they would also focus on other issues.
articles.body: Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told NBC’s “Meet the Press” Sunday that President Donald Trump has “undoubtedly” committed impeachable offenses but that Democrats would also focus on issues like healthcare if they win back the House. “Everybody on our side understands that impeachment is a critical tool in the toolbox for constitutional self-defense against a president acting like a king, an imperious, lawless, arrogant king,” Raskin said, responding to a question about whether Democrats should move to impeach Trump if they retake the House. He added, though, that Trump’s two impeachments constituted half of all impeachments in U.S. history, noting that after the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol, Democrats were unable to persuade enough Republicans to side with them to convict the president. Trump has been impeached twice, though he has never been convicted. As midterm elections approach, Democrats have not closed the door on moving to impeach Trump again if they retake the House. Trump, too, has warned his supporters that Democrats could try to impeach him again. Moderator Kristen Welker pressed Raskin again on his stance toward impeachment, and Raskin said that “impeachment is not a taboo with us.” “It’s not a fetish with us,” he said. “We understand it’s not a panacea. It is a tool in the toolbox. We will not hesitate to use it if we need to use it.” Raskin, who previously served as a lead impeachment manager against Trump, said that the president had “undoubtedly” committed impeachable offenses in his second term, adding: “We don’t have time to remotely scratch the surface.” “But going to war without a declaration of war, for example, continually defying Congress in terms of our appropriation of money, stealing our spending power from us,” he continued. “I mean, I would say even just bulldozing the East Wing of the White House. If he can bulldoze the East Wing, he can bulldoze the West Wing. He believes that he is a king. They’ve been plundering money from our government in the most massively corrupt presidential administration in American history.” Raskin added that “nothing comes close to the kind of plunder and corruption we’ve been seeing in this administration, and all of that could warrant an impeachment investigation if we wanted to do it.” “But more important to us right now is getting healthcare to the American people and ending the lawlessness,” he said. Trump has warned Republicans that if they do not win in the midterms, Democrats would “find a reason to impeach me.” Trump was impeached for the first time in 2019 over allegations that he pressured Ukraine to investigate Joe Biden and his son while withholding hundreds of millions of dollars in aid. He was impeached for a second time after the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol. The president was acquitted both times. Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., said last month on “Meet the Press” that Democrats should not make impeaching Trump a priority if they regain the House majority. Instead, he said, Democrats’ priority should be “making housing, education, energy, healthcare affordable and accessible for all of our citizens.” “Impeaching the president will not do that,” he added. In June, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said on “Meet the Press” that Democrats “haven’t ruled anything in or ruled anything out in terms of accountability” when asked about whether his party would try to impeach Trump if they win the House. “What we have said is that our focus is going to be to make life more affordable for the American people,” he said at the time.

articles.title: The Faster Labor Contracts Act would give workers a fair shot at a better life
articles.summary: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick called on the Senate to pass the Faster Labor Contracts Act to expedite collective bargaining and protect the economic security of working families.
articles.body:
Labor Day reminds me of a moment in my childhood. I couldn’t have been more than five years old, sitting on my grandfather’s knee and listening to stories about his journey from Ireland through Ellis Island. He taught me more than family history. He taught me what hard work could make possible — and how his membership in the Iron Workers union gave him the security and opportunity to build the better life he had crossed an ocean in search of.

For too many families today, that dream has slipped out of reach. The Faster Labor Contracts Act is one way I am working to restore it — by giving workers a fairer path to the security, opportunity and upward mobility that helped change the course of my own family.

The pressures facing working families are not abstract. Housing, health care, education, childcare and everyday necessities consume more of the family budget. Wages have struggled to keep pace. And even workers who exercise their legal right to organize can spend months — or years — waiting for their first contract that actually moves them forward.

A new Gallup report shows labor unions with a 71 percent approval rating, the highest in recent history, with support extending across Independents, Republicans and Democrats. It’s easy to understand why. Research shows that union workers earn over 11 percent more than their nonunion peers and are more likely to have employer-sponsored health coverage and access to paid sick leave.

Yet only 10 percent of Americans belong to unions today.

When workers seek to organize, they can face sophisticated anti-union campaigns, designed to discourage them from exercising that right. Where these tactics fail, some employers refuse to bargain in good faith altogether. As a result, it takes almost a year and a half on average for workers to negotiate a first contract.

The consequences extend well beyond the bargaining table. The decline in union membership has coincided with the eroding standard of living for middle-class families. As bargaining power for workers has decreased, we’ve seen income inequality skyrocket, wages stagnate, and less economic mobility than ever before.

This is not the American Dream that brought my family away from the emerald shores of Ireland, and it’s not the American Dream working families yearn for as they agonize over how to afford a home, educate their children, pay their medical bills, or simply keep pace with the rising cost of everyday life.

The Faster Labor Contracts Act would address one of the clearest failures in the current system. It would require employers to begin bargaining within 10 days of notification from a new union. If an agreement isn’t reached after 90 days of good-faith negotiations, the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service would step in unless both parties agree to extend negotiations. If mediation still fails to produce an agreement, federal arbitrators could then issue a binding two-year decision to resolve the impasse.

I have seen the importance of that principle firsthand in my own community, Pennsylvania’s 1st District. When our nurses at St. Mary Medical Center in Bucks County voted to organize, I supported their decision and their right to have a meaningful voice in the workplace.

The same standard should apply wherever Pennsylvania workers choose to organize. At UPMC Magee-Women’s Hospital in Pittsburgh, nearly 1,000 nurses and advanced practitioners voted last year to form a union and strengthen their voice for their patients and profession. In first-contract negotiations, they have sought stronger staffing standards, compensation that helps retain experienced nurses, and expanded benefits, including parental leave. More than a year later, they remain without an agreement.

That is where the Faster Labor Contracts Act matters. A vote to organize should begin a meaningful bargaining process, not an indefinite waiting game. When workers have made their choice and come to the table in good faith, delay should not be allowed to render that choice meaningless.

That same commitment to protecting the economic security of working families is also driving my work with SEIU on the Good Jobs for Good Airports Act . Across the Philadelphia region, airport service workers can lose hard-earned wages and benefits simply because a new contractor takes over. A change in contractor should not mean a step backward for the people doing the work. In both cases, the principle is simple: Hard work should still provide a fair path to stability, opportunity and a better future.

Working Americans are facing a rising cost of living, wages that have struggled to keep pace, and an economy in which too many families feel they are working harder simply to tread water. We need the Faster Labor Contracts Act to restore balance, strengthen workers’ bargaining power, and ensure that choosing to organize leads to a fair and timely first contract.

This Labor Day, the Senate has an opportunity to renew a basic American promise: that hard work should still lead to a better life. I call on my colleagues to pass the FLCA, stand on the side of American workers, and help ensure that promise remains within reach for the next generation.

Brian Fitzpatrick represents Pennsylvania’s 1st Congressional District in the U.S. House of Representatives.

articles.title: Michigan’s controversial win adds to the nagging feeling college football just isn’t fair
articles.summary: Apparently, the Big House is the land where time stands still; Michigan’s controversial win adds to the nagging feeling college football just isn’t fair
articles.body: Apparently, the Big House is the land where time stands still, where clocks melt like a Salvador Dalí painting and Deloreans wind back the minute hand just enough for the home team to get another chance. It’s where games end but somehow continue, where football takes 60 minutes and one second and days are 24 hours and one second. Where teams already afforded every advantage are now given the gift of imaginary time. That is the real travesty in Western Michigan’s 13-12 “loss” to Michigan. The Broncos seemed to have pulled off the biggest win in school history only for the official to add one second back on the clock for one last play, in which Michigan completed a Hail Mary pass for the win. This entire offseason has felt like a protracted exercise in gluttony. The conferences, schools, players and coaches who already have so much still want more, and when they can’t get it, they go to court to get their way. LSU poleaxed a team that used to win national championships on the regular, and somehow still thinks it needs the assistance of would-be-but-couldn’t-make-it NFL dudes. The SEC and Big Ten asked Congress for help to bail them out of the mess they had created, looking for ways to curtail outrageous spending and put guardrails up on the college athletics Autobahn. So, Congress came up with a solution, but the two leagues dithered over the particulars just long enough that the Protect College Sports Act never really had a chance. Look, the playing fields haven’t been even in decades, the gap between the moneyed schools widening with each passing season. But the advent of NIL has turned the gap into an unconquerable chasm. According to the U.S. Department of Education Equity in Athletics website, Western Michigan’s budget – for its entire department – is $8 million. Published reports estimate Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood’s NIL package at between $10.5 million and $12.5 million over four years. When lettermen sweaters are stitched with gold threading and designed by Armani, it makes the whole thing a little harder to stomach. But all of that distaste was supposed to go away when the games began, when the undefeated and delicious product that is college football finally got the chance to shove the ancillary stuff back into the shadows. Instead, here we are, a week in and wondering why an official review is seemingly being run like a Louisiana courtroom. Why the eleventh hour came with an extra second, killing time proved impossible, and time fails to fly in Ann Arbor. So absurdly controversial was the final not-last second call, it’s temporarily dislodged Lane Kiffin from the spot of top of the most reviled man in football. “When I looked up at the clock, it was past zeroes,’’ said Western Michigan head coach Lance Taylor. Because it was. Time had officially run out on Michigan, the 24th-ranked Wolverines held to a baseball score by their directional little brother over in Kalamazoo. Underwood’s last-ditch pass sailed out of bounds, the clock clearly showing zero before the ball touched a Western Michigan defender’s hand. Officials called for an immediate review, a fair and reasonable request on a last-second play. And then they went into the Delorean and found a second that didn’t exist. Given a redo, Underwood made a hero 47-yard throw that JJ Buchanan somehow snatched out of traffic as he fell into the end zone. Late Saturday night, the Big Ten released a statement and explanation, saying that a Western Michigan player had touched the ball with one second left. They released video and audio to coincide with the statement, though it is not clear why the clock they used was entirely different than what was seen both on TV and in the stadium. It’s also difficult to tell, because the defender has his back to the camera, when exactly he touched the ball. At best it was a nanosecond or so of difference. The odds of the Big Ten overturning the call were always going to be steeper than the +27.5-point spread the Broncos faced against the Wolverines. If the league was to say the call was wrong, it would have to negate Michigan’s victory. And let’s be real: If Michigan didn’t vacate any wins after the whole Connor Stalions’ caper, they aren’t losing this one. Western Michigan and the MAC took the high road. Both said they accepted the Big Ten’s explanation, and Taylor was a model of decorum in his postgame comments. Still, it begs the public to dismiss something it saw with its own eyes. At the very least, in a world of technological advances, there needs to be better synchronization with the officials’ clock and the one in stadium. That doesn’t seem so much to ask. The real kick here is this isn’t even the first time this happened with Michigan. In 2005, officials found two seconds when the unranked Wolverines hosted No. 8 Penn State. Back then, they ruled the stadium clock stopped too early after Michigan was granted a timeout. On the next play, quarterback Chad Henne threw a 10-yard TD pass to Mario Manningham, giving the Wolverines the win. The difference is, Penn State went on to win the rest of its games and earn an invite to the Orange Bowl. There won’t be other chances like this for Western Michigan. The Broncos’ next opponent is Monmouth, followed by Rice and Boise State before they roll headlong into MAC play. This was their chance. To steal from another sport where Cinderella gets more of an opportunity than in college football, it was their one shining moment. Instead time, as it turns out, does wait for some teams. For Michigan, in the Big House, it happily stands still.

articles.title: Sen. John Kennedy criticizes the Trump administration’s approach to Putin amid latest peace talks
articles.summary: Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., criticized Republican leadership on a number of issues including the Trump administration’s approach to ending the war in Ukraine, calling ongoing negotiations in Kyiv and Moscow “pretty talk,” that likely won’t end the war
articles.body: Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., criticized Republican leadership on a number of issues including the Trump administration’s handling of the Ukraine peace process and Senate leaders’ response to inflation woes. Kennedy told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” on Sunday he believes the Trump administration should take a different approach to Russian President Vladimir Putin. “This guy’s a pirate. He’s got blood under his fingernails. He doesn’t care about a bunch of pretty talk,” Kennedy said Sunday, as U.S. envoys meet with leaders on both sides of the conflict. “You don’t get any credit for kissing his ass. You’ve got to show him you mean business.” Last week, the House failed to pass a Russian sanctions bill that the Senate approved in August. “We should have passed that Russian sanctions bill, and we’ve got another chance to do it,” the Louisiana senator said. “Then we ought to help Ukraine and help Europe. They’re doing OK on their own, but we can provide them intelligence.” Kennedy’s comments come as President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and the president’s special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Putin in Russia and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv this weekend. “We got Putin down. We’re choking him to death. We’re choking him. We’ve got to choke him to death. That’s what he understands,” the senator added. “I’m not putting down any of the talk, and I think talk is good and it can be helpful. But I won’t faint with surprise if our guys don’t come out of there without a deal.” Kennedy also weighed in on the ongoing military conflict with Iran, telling “Meet the Press” moderator Kristen Welker that the war will “probably not” end before the upcoming midterm elections. Still, he praised the Trump administration’s decision to launch the military conflict, telling Welker: “We have accomplished all of our objectives in Iran. ... There’s just one problem: the Strait [of Hormuz] is semi-closed.” The senator said that with the strait still blockaded by the U.S. military, gas prices in the U.S. likely won’t drop soon. “The blockade was a smart play. It’s hurting the Iranians badly. It’s hurting the government,” Kennedy said. “I think we ought to leave it on for a few more months if we can stand the pain at the pump.” Kennedy on Sunday also expressed doubt that Republicans in Congress would be able to do anything to lower costs or tackle inflation before November’s midterm elections, lightly criticizing his own leadership for not dealing with the issue sooner. He described the economy as “solid” and pointed to “low” unemployment numbers, but said that inflation is “a big if.” “It’s gutting people like a fish. Inflation is pernicious. And we’ve had it for a few years now. It’s been up and down since President Biden’s administration,” Kennedy said. “What we ought to do is something about it. I’m not blaming it on the president or the House. The Senate Republicans, about five months ago, for a reconciliation bill, we should have addressed it. We didn’t for a couple reasons. Number one, I couldn’t convince the majority leader to put a bill like that on the floor. And number two, we’re probably three or four votes short.” Asked whether Republicans have enough time to address inflation before the midterm elections, Kennedy said, “We can do anything we want to in reconciliation and ask the House to come back and do it.” Kennedy highlighted a procedural move Senate Republicans could use to pass some legislation without support from Senate Democrats but cast doubt on whether they would. “I’m not saying we will do that, certainly based on our record the last five or six months. It’s not likely.”

articles.title: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to allow mail ballot restrictions to move forward for a third time
articles.summary: The Trump administration on Sunday asked the Supreme Court to temporarily allow the U.S.
articles.body: The Trump administration on Sunday asked the Supreme Court to temporarily allow the U.S. Postal Service to exert some control over mail-in voting in the upcoming midterm elections, just two days after a federal judge blocked the USPS from doing so. It’s the third time the Trump administration has escalated this matter to the Supreme Court, as North Carolina last week became the first state to begin sending mail-in ballots to voters less than 60 days before the midterm elections. On Friday, U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani issued an order preventing the administration from carrying out the Trump-directed USPS regulation on mail-in ballots. The directive is the president’s latest attempt to impose new forms of federal control over elections, which are typically run by states. It would allow the USPS to track mail-in ballots and potentially reject ballots that are sent to and from voters not included in a federal database. This application to the court comes after Talwani issued a preliminary block on enforcing the USPS rule, saying it’s likely unlawful and unconstitutional for the federal government to dictate how mail-in ballots are handled. In her order Friday, Talwani also cited the rushed nature of the rule, writing that the “immediate implementation of the Final Rule issued less than seventy days before the November 2026 election threatens disenfranchisement of millions of United States citizens who seek to vote by mail.” In Sunday’s filing to the Supreme Court, the Trump administration argued: “Contrary to the claims of the district court and respondents that the Postal Service is trying to federalize the rules for mail-in voting, the Postal Service’s final rule imposes only modest envelope-design and addressee-information requirements for federal-election ballots sent via U.S. Mail.” Specifically, the filing argues, the rule “requires States to upload the name, address, and barcode information of intended recipients of ballot mail in an online portal — information that election officials would necessarily already possess to send ballot mail under the Rule to those recipients.” “The Rule ensures that States remain responsible for determining voter eligibility and eligibility to vote by mail, and it does not dictate ballot content, mailing or receipt deadlines, or ballot-counting procedures. The Rule thus plainly does not seize control of States’ administration of elections — it simply imposes reasonable preparation requirements for certain election-related mail,” the filing adds. Sunday’s application to the Supreme Court comes after the Trump administration already twice asked the highest court to intervene in this case. The Justice Department withdrew its previous pending request after submitting this morning’s application related to Talwani’s most recent order. The rule stems from a March executive order signed by President Donald Trump. It came just weeks after the president suggested that Republicans should “nationalize” elections, a comment that drew criticism from local election officials and lawmakers from Trump’s own party.

articles.title: DOJ makes new appeal for Supreme Court to allow mail voting changes
articles.summary: The Trump administration on Sunday again asked the Supreme Court to allow it to restrict mail-in voting this election cycle. In a 40-page emergency application, Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the justices to immediately permit the administration to bar the U.S. Postal Service from sending mail-in ballots to residents of states that have not…
articles.body:
The Trump administration on Sunday again asked the Supreme Court to allow it to restrict mail-in voting this election cycle.

In a 40-page emergency application , Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the justices to immediately permit the administration to bar the U.S. Postal Service from sending mail-in ballots to residents of states that have not submitted a list of eligible voters based on citizenship data.

Sauer argued the administration is likely to succeed on the merits in two cases concerning the policy — one a group of Democratic-led states brought against the Postal Service and another the League of Women Voters of Massachusetts brought against the administration.

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani on Friday indefinitely halted the Postal Service’s plan while lower courts decided on the policy. Her ruling came on the day North Carolina began to mail ballots to residents, which Sauer noted in his Sunday filing.

Talwani, an appointee of former President Obama, halted the administration from carrying out the plan a day after Sauer submitted an initial stay application to the Supreme Court. But in filing the administration’s new request for a stay of Talwani’s preliminary injunction, the solicitor general withdrew his Thursday filing.

The Supreme Court, which is on recess, will decide the case in an expedited fashion. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, one of the three liberals on the high court, was assigned to the administration’s new request.

In his Sunday filing, Sauer wrote the policy “is a valid exercise” of the Postal Service’s authority, and “does not regulate state administration” of elections.

“The Rule ensures that States remain responsible for determining voter eligibility and eligibility to vote by mail, and it does not dictate ballot content, mailing or receipt deadlines, or ballot-counting procedures,” he wrote.

“The Rule thus plainly does not seize control of States’ administration of elections — it simply imposes reasonable preparation requirements for certain election-related mail,” Sauer added.

But Sophia Lin Lakin, the director of the American Civil Liberties Union’s Voting Rights Projects, blasted the Postal Service’s policy as “unconstitutional” and accused the Trump administration of “running” to the Supreme Court to circumvent lower court rulings earlier this week.

“The only emergency here is the one the administration created,” added Lakin, whose organization is representing some of the challengers to the administration’s rule. “The court’s temporary order preserves the voting procedures Americans have relied on for years, and it should stand.”
