articles.title: Sanders pushes 'death penalty' for crucial US industry that could give advantage to foreign adversaries
articles.summary: Progressives on Capitol Hill are pushing a proposal to ban artificial superintelligence, but critics warn the move could hand global tech dominance over to China and Russia.
articles.body: Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, introduced legislation Thursday seeking to hit American artificial intelligence developers with a "corporate death penalty" and up to 20 years in prison— a move critics warn will hand a crucial edge in the global AI arms race to Beijing and Moscow. The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act would temporarily halt advanced AI development and establish a Cabinet-level federal agency authorized to oversee the physical destruction of non-compliant tech systems, likening advanced AI creation to the unlawful development of nuclear weapons. The measure explicitly targets systems capable of matching or exceeding human cognitive performance—specifically outlawing any AI model that exhibits the capacity to subvert shutdown commands, execute unauthorized cyberattacks, or undermine the U.S. government. But while progressives frame the measure as an urgent check on "AI oligarchs," experts are warning that imposing sweeping criminal penalties on U.S. firms will severely handicap domestic innovation, while foreign adversaries will be able to continue expanding their capabilities unchecked. FETTERMAN ALIGNS WITH TRUMP ON AI PUSH, WARNS CHINA BENEFITS FROM US 'OVERREACTION' "If the United States stops developing advanced AI, China is unlikely to follow. Surrendering the lead in a potentially transformative technology would carry serious economic and national security costs," Daniel Castro, president of the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation (ITIF), a leading nonpartisan tech-innovation policy think tank, said in response to Sanders' proposal. "A permanent, unilateral ban on all research into superhuman AI is too broad," added Gary Marcus, an AI expert who has testified on the matter before the U.S. Senate. He added that the proposed law was "a guarantee" the U.S. would be left behind when it comes to artificial intelligence advancements, describing it as "not the right approach," even though he said there were some aspects of the proposed bill that were "defensible." REP. TED LIEU: AI IS ALREADY TOO POWERFUL. WE NEED A KILL SWITCH BEFORE DISASTER STRIKES Under the provisions of the legislation, the proposed criminal and corporate penalties are modeled directly after existing federal statutes governing the unlawful development of nuclear weapons. Tech companies found attempting to circumvent the federal prohibition would face a "corporate death penalty"—an unprecedented enforcement mechanism that strips a firm's legal authority to conduct business in the United States. Individual software engineers, researchers or executives found in violation could face up to 20 years in federal prison. DEM SENATOR PRESSES OPENAI, ANTHROPIC FOR ANSWERS IN AI HACKING PROBE To enforce the ban, the legislation creates a new Cabinet-level federal AI agency tasked with monitoring frontier systems. The agency would be granted sweeping authority to intervene in tech operations, including physically supervising the removal of dangerous code and overseeing the physical destruction of non-compliant superintelligent hardware and infrastructure. The bill also establishes criteria for what constitutes a banned system, specifically outlawing any AI model capable of planning or executing the "disempowerment of humanity." That includes software that exhibits the capacity to overthrow the U.S. government, carry out unauthorized cyberattacks or ignore human shutdown commands. CRACKDOWN ON CRITICAL TECH COULD OPEN AMERICANS TO A NEW NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT Industry advocates, however, argue that resorting to extreme criminal sanctions ignores the practical realities of tech infrastructure and risk management. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Knee-jerk policymaking is never a good thing, and I think that’s exactly what this proposal boils down to," said Aden Hizkias, associate policy director at Chamber of Progress, a tech industry coalition. "AI is an incredible tool that can improve millions of lives, but as AI skepticism grows, it’s on companies to earn trust and prove they are good neighbors. That means transparent construction agreements, bringing their own power generation, and making sure they're meeting environmental standards." Fox News Digital reached out to Sanders' office for comment regarding concerns that the legislation would hand an AI edge to foreign adversaries like China and Russia, but did not receive a response in time for publication.

articles.title: AfD has 'made history' in Saxony-Anhalt, says lead candidate Siegmund
articles.summary: The Alternative for Germany (AfD) has "made history" in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund said on Sunday after exit polls sh...
articles.body:
Alternative for Germany (AfD) secures 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt state election, narrowly missing an absolute majority in the state parliament.

AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund aims to become the party's first premier in one of Germany's federal states.

Despite its historic win, AfD faces challenges forming a ruling coalition due to other mainstream parties' refusal to work with them.

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) has "made history" in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund said on Sunday after exit polls showed the far-right party securing 44% of the vote.

"We have achieved exactly what we wanted to achieve," Siegmund said after the first exit polls were announced by broadcaster ARD. "We have made history in this state."

Siegmund is hoping to become the AfD's first premier of one of Germany's 16 federal states, but the exit polls suggest the party has narrowly missed securing an absolute majority in the state parliament in Magdeburg.

Siegmund, who became a political sensation on the campaign trail in Saxony-Anhalt, said he wanted to extend a hand to all parties willing to bring about a fundamental political transformation in the state. However, the AfD will not bend to other parties' will, he stressed.

The AfD has never participated in a ruling coalition in Germany's 16 states or its federal government, as all other mainstream parties refuse to work with it, a policy infamously known as the "firewall."

articles.title: Trump official says ‘there may not be a nuclear agreement’ with Iran
articles.summary: US Energy Secretary Chris Wright’s comments could signal that US hopes for a nuclear deal are dimming.
articles.body:
As the United States and Iran resume trading attacks, a top US official has publicly downplayed the chances of one of President Donald Trump’s initial key objectives in the US and Israel’s war on Iran: getting a signed nuclear agreement .

During an interview on Sunday with US channel ABC News, the US Energy Secretary, Chris Wright, said “there may not” be a nuclear deal, signalling that the US may pivot instead to launching strikes against any Iranian efforts to build nuclear infrastructure.

“It may be simply destroying their capabilities to do it,” Wright said on ‘ABC This Week’ about Iran’s ambitions to obtain a nuclear weapon.

The US has previously targeted facilities it said had been used to support Iran’s nuclear programme. Iran has always maintained that it is developing a nuclear power programme only and does not have plans to build a nuclear weapon.

Later, when pressed by the show’s co-host, Martha Raddatz, on whether the US would resort to continued bombing instead of diplomacy, Wright defended US actions in Iran.

“They don’t have the capability to build more missiles,” Wright said. “We’re degrading their capacity to develop nuclear weapons and, ultimately, to deliver them if they develop them.”

However, the former oil executive whose agency oversees the US stockpile of nuclear weapons said that a deal with Iran could be possible under new leadership.

“An agreement may await the next administration in Iran,” he said. “We simply don’t know that.”

The Trump administration official’s comments could signal that US hopes for a nuclear deal are dimming and slipping further out of reach.

After the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran collapsed in July, attacks paused, then resumed, coupled with Iranian closures of the Strait of Hormuz and US naval blockade.

Despite recent exchanges of intense fire between US and Iranian forces, the White House has attempted to minimise the conflict in public remarks.

On Friday, Trump sought to downplay the war in Iran, calling it “small potatoes”. While at a White House news briefing on Thursday, Vice President JD Vance appeared to suggest that the conflict had cooled and to shrug off an alleged US attack on a wedding in southern Iran, saying “ sometimes things happen “.

At a White House briefing this week, Vance said of the conflict that he “wouldn’t call it a war” and there was “no active shooting right now”.

Without offering specifics, Wright on Sunday said the US would “get the job done” in Iran and other nations would be offering their help to bring an end to the war.

“We will work in cooperation with our allies in the region,” Wright said. “I think you’ll see countries from around the world joining this effort as well.”

Al Jazeera has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: Washington’s affordability debate is missing wages
articles.summary: The article argues that a comprehensive affordability agenda must go beyond lowering prices to ensure workers earn enough to live through higher wages and collective bargaining power.
articles.body:
When Angelica Hernandez joined a union, her McDonald’s manager warned her that the company had an army of lawyers, the union would rob her, and she would end up living under a bridge. For three years, Hernandez had resisted joining, afraid of retaliation or losing her job. What finally pushed her to sign on was the intimidation itself.

“If I end up living under a bridge,” she remembered thinking, “I’m going to fight to make sure it doesn’t happen to others.”

Her story contains the missing half of America’s affordability debate. Politicians talk about making rent, groceries, health care, and child care cheaper. They talk much less about whether workers earn enough to keep pace.

With the midterms approaching, affordability has become the defining economic issue of American politics. But it is too often framed as a crisis of prices alone, as though paychecks were fixed and the only solution was to make things cheaper.

Prices and wages come down to the same question: Does a job pay enough to live?

The Fight for $15 forced that question onto the national agenda. When roughly 200 fast-food workers walked off their jobs in New York City in November 2012, they sought more than double the federal minimum wage. The demand was dismissed as unserious. President Obama was calling for a $9 minimum wage ; leading Democrats considered $10.10 ambitious . Yet workers chose a number that reflected what survival required rather than what Washington considered plausible.

By the end of 2026, 79 jurisdictions will have reached or exceeded a $15 minimum wage. The National Employment Law Project estimates that the movement helped produce $150 billion in raises for 26 million workers. It also widened the fight to include predictable schedules, paid sick leave, and a voice in setting standards.

The movement taught the country that a winning wage demand cannot remain frozen in time. Adjusted for inflation, the $15 workers demanded in 2012 would be worth about $21.65 today. Yet the federal minimum remains at $7.25, where it has been since 2009, even as roughly 14 million workers still earn less than $15 an hour.

In June 2026, 55 percent of Oklahoma voters rejected a ballot measure that would have raised the state minimum wage from $7.25 to $15 by 2029 and indexed it to the cost of living thereafter.

Opponents argued that the increase would destroy jobs and raise prices. The defeat showed how easily the language of affordability can be turned against higher wages.

The Fight for $15 also fell short of its full promise. It won enormous wage gains without winning widespread collective-bargaining rights for fast-food workers. Workers who became public faces of the campaign did not always gain a permanent role in the institutions making decisions about their lives. I had encountered that dynamic before. During the 2024 presidential campaign, I organized across Arizona, including Native communities that national politicians often visit when electoral margins are close and leave once votes are counted. On a trip to Havasupai, the tribal chairwoman described years of underinvestment. As we prepared to leave, she took my hand and told me something I have not forgotten. “When you are in a room with power, bring us into it.”

I had understood her words as a charge to carry a community’s concerns into powerful rooms.

Listening later to worker leaders from the Fight for $15 describe what happened after the strikes ended and the cameras disappeared, I understood them differently. Being heard by those with power is different from possessing power yourself.

A credible affordability agenda must address both wages and the power workers need to secure them. Congress should set a meaningful national wage floor and index it to inflation or the national median wage. States should retain the ability to set higher standards where living costs demand them. But wage laws alone are not enough. Workers need institutions that give them an enduring voice.

California’s Fast-Food Council , which brings workers, employers, and public officials into the process of setting industry standards, offers one model. Stronger unions, sector-wide bargaining, worker standards boards, and enforceable protections against retaliation offer others.

This is where the affordability agenda has been thinnest. A tax credit can deliver relief. A price cap can reduce a bill. A minimum-wage law can increase a paycheck. Yet, none of those policies gives working people the collective power to shape the next decision, enforce the last one, or prevent their gains from being eroded.

Candidates running on affordability this fall should answer three questions: What wage should a full-time job pay? What mechanism will keep that wage from losing value? And what institutions will give workers the power to defend it after Election Day?

The Fight for $15 supplied the missing logic in today’s affordability debate. Its central insight is that economic security depends on what people earn as well as what they pay. The danger is that politicians will embrace that insight while leaving behind the workers who gave it meaning.

Hernandez learned that asking for more became less frightening once she no longer had to ask alone. A true affordability agenda would carry that lesson forward. A job should pay enough to build a life, and workers should possess enough power to defend what they build.

Dylan Baca is a researcher, writer and former political organizer who has led youth and Native voter engagement efforts in Arizona and nationally. Baca is a graduate of Columbia University, where he studied political science and American studies.

On Thursday, Sept. 28, 2023, Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a law giving fast food workers a $20 minimum wage on April 1, 2024. (AP Photo/Terry Chea, File)

articles.title: Trump admin’s mail-in ballot fight lands back at Supreme Court
articles.summary: The Trump administration asks the Supreme Court to enforce postal service ballot mail restrictions as North Carolina ballots already enter the mail.
articles.body: The Trump administration filed a new appeal with the Supreme Court on Sunday seeking to enforce restrictions on mail ballots, as the ballots begin entering states across the country ahead of the midterm elections. The filing asks the high court to stay a preliminary injunction issued Friday by U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani that prevents the U.S. Postal Service from enforcing several requirements for ballot mail in the November elections. "Ballots have already begun to be mailed in North Carolina, and more States will begin the mailing process as the injunction remains in place — including Alabama on September 9 and at least five States the week of September 13," Solicitor General John Sauer wrote. FEDERAL JUDGE AGAIN BLOCKS TRUMP'S MAIL BALLOT ORDER JUST BEFORE MIDTERMS "Once those ballot envelopes enter the mailstream, there is no retrieving them," he added. Sauer argued that allowing the injunction to remain in place risks "sowing confusion and chaos" as more states begin mailing ballots because preparations to comply with the Postal Service rule remain voluntary rather than mandatory. The administration maintains the rule is "a lawful and modest exercise of rulemaking authority delegated by Congress to the Postal Service" and "regulates the U.S. Mail, not federal elections." The rule requires federal election ballots sent through the mail to use envelopes that include the official Election Mail logo, meet automation requirements and carry unique barcodes, according to the filing. State election officials would also have to submit envelope designs for review and provide the Postal Service with information about intended ballot recipients. The administration says the requirements are intended to improve the handling and delivery of ballot mail and protect the mail system from being used to facilitate voter fraud. MAIL-VOTING CRACKDOWN MOVES AHEAD AS TRUMP COURT WIN OPENS DOOR TO FEDERAL ACTION The rule would not give the Postal Service authority to determine who is eligible to vote by mail or whether ballots should be counted, responsibilities that would remain with state and local election officials. Democratic-led states and voting rights groups challenging the restrictions contend the changes are unconstitutional, while election officials have argued there is not enough time to revise their systems to comply before November. The administration disputes those arguments, saying Congress gave the Postal Service broad authority to regulate the handling and delivery of mail and that the rule does not dictate ballot content, determine voter eligibility, establish election deadlines or govern how ballots are counted. The filing marks the third time the administration has asked the Supreme Court to intervene in the dispute. The high court previously allowed the administration’s plan to move forward but has not ruled on whether the restrictions themselves are legal. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The battle could have major ramifications for the November elections, when control of Congress is at stake. Nearly one-third of U.S. voters cast ballots by mail. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Carr: FCC ‘looking at a lot of actions’ to stop broadcasters’ partisan coverage
articles.summary: Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chair Brendan Carr on Sunday said he is “looking at a lot of actions” to prevent networks from airing fake polls and partisan coverage ahead of midterm elections. Carr appeared on Fox News’s “The Sunday Briefing” with Peter Doocy and said that networks are intended to operate in the public interest…
articles.body:
Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chair Brendan Carr on Sunday said he is “looking at a lot of actions” to prevent networks from airing fake polls and partisan coverage ahead of midterm elections.

Carr appeared on Fox News’s “The Sunday Briefing” with Peter Doocy and said that networks are intended to operate in the public interest and “not some sort of narrow partisan interest.”

“I think President Trump is over the target, and we’re looking at a lot of actions,” he continued. “For instance, there’s a lot of interest right now in fake polls that are out there and so the FCC may put guidance out soon to remind broadcasters about their obligations with respect to not air fake polls, particularly if they’re done to suppress people heading into the fall.”

His comments come after President Trump urged the agency to punish NBC News’s Kristen Welker. She angered the president last Sunday while teasing an upcoming episode of “Meet the Press” on its Washington, D.C., affiliate earlier in the day. She said Trump is “going to loom large over” the midterm elections while also noting that Trump-endorsed candidates have had “mixed results” during the Republican primaries.

Trump has compiled a 96-percent winning record in this year’s primaries, according to Ballotpedia. Those who have lost include Georgia Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, Rep. Randy Feenstra (R-Iowa), MyPillow founder Mike Lindell and South Carolina Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette.

“How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves?” Trump wrote last week on Truth Social. “Results are attached. Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment.”

NBC News said it stands by Welker, calling her “one of the best in the business.”

Trump has frequently called on the FCC, historically an independent commission, to apply pressure on leading broadcasters throughout his second term. Carr has launched investigations into NBC and ABC’s diversity, equity and inclusion hiring practices.

He and Trump have praised CBS News under its new editor Bar Weiss, previously a columnist, as the network is under parent company Paramount Skydance, led by Trump ally and billionaire David Ellison.

Critics have denounced the president’s use of the FCC as a tool to intimidate journalists ahead of the midterms.

Some Republicans, however, have warned against enforcing regulatory penalties on broadcasters, particularly over ABC’s actions after Jimmy Kimmel was suspended for comments he made after conservative activist Charlie Kirk was killed last September.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), chair of the Senate Commerce Committee, warned last year that Carr’s threats of action against ABC were “dangerous as hell.”

articles.summary: Pennsylvania Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) said Sunday he “might” mount a primary challenge to Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) in 2028. “I might, I haven’t decided that. And to be really blunt, I’m doing everything I can right now to help Democrats in Pennsylvania flip congressional seats to give [Pennsylvania Gov.] Josh Shapiro a governing majority…
articles.body:
Pennsylvania Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) said Sunday he “might” mount a primary challenge to Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) in 2028.

“I might, I haven’t decided that. And to be really blunt, I’m doing everything I can right now to help Democrats in Pennsylvania flip congressional seats to give [Pennsylvania Gov.] Josh Shapiro a governing majority in the state Senate and grow the majority in the state House,” Deluzio told host Chris Stirewalt on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday.”

Deluzio later said, “John Fetterman’s nowhere to be seen on the campaign trail. And again, to be very blunt, I don’t think there’s any Democrat in Pennsylvania who wants him campaigning with them, even if he wouldn’t show up.

“So I’m focused on doing what we can do right now to win, and I’ll deal with 2028 when we get past the [midterms].”

Democrats inside and outside of Pennsylvania have taken Fetterman to task throughout the last 18 months, as the first-term senator has sided with President Trump and the GOP on multiple issues — including on the Iran war, with Fetterman voting against every Senate war powers resolution introduced in the upper chamber.

Criticism of Fetterman also ramped up after The Wall Street Journal published a piece on Friday outlining Fetterman’s alleged lack of commitment to his duties as a senator. Fetterman has blasted the report as a “hit piece.”

Deluzio was among those to criticize Fetterman, saying Friday that Fetterman “has no sense of duty” to his constituents.

“He is not up for the high office he was elected to — and we in Pennsylvania will do something about it in 2028,” the second-term representative wrote on social platform X .

Fetterman has also criticized his party’s turn against Israel, defending the Israeli military’s campaign in Gaza. Fetterman said in June his party abandoning the country’s Middle Eastern ally would be a red line.

“If our party ever becomes — and just makes it official — the anti-Israel party, that’s when I would leave,” he told Alexander Bolton at the Hill Nation Summit.

Roughly half of Democrats believe that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza, according to a poll conducted in June by The Associated Press and NORC Center for Public Affairs Research.

Last year, Fetterman voted in line with Trump’s position 28 percent of the time, the most of any Senate Democrat, per data from VoteHub .

articles.title: Hinojosa on Trump $10 million Paxton race investment: ‘I welcome the attention on Texas’
articles.summary: Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa (D) embraced the new spotlight on her state brought on by the unexpectedly close Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton. “You are running in a state President Trump won by nearly 14 percentage points. He just announced, as I mentioned, that $10 million investment to boost…
articles.body:
Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa (D) embraced the new spotlight on her state brought on by the unexpectedly close Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton.

“You are running in a state President Trump won by nearly 14 percentage points. He just announced, as I mentioned, that $10 million investment to boost Republican chances in the Texas Senate race. Are you concerned that all of this will, in fact, energize GOP voters in Texas?” CNN’s Dana Bash asked Hinojosa, a representative in the state’s House.

“No, actually not at all. If you look at the polling, President Trump is underwater, Greg Abbott is underwater and people are tired of this politics as usual. People want change in Texas. They’re galvanizing, organizing. We’re building real momentum in this race,” the Democrat replied.

She added, “So, I welcome the attention on Texas. Texas is battleground in 2026. If you don’t believe it, look at what Republicans are doing. But that’s what I hear every day on the campaign trail.”

Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., gave $10 million to the Texas attorney general’s Senate campaign , per Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings published over the weekend.

In a poll from late last month, incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott (R) was leading Hinojosa in the race by 7 percentage points, earning 48 percent of respondents’ support. Just 1 percent of those polled backed the Libertarian third-party candidate, while the remaining 8 percent were undecided and 1 percent said they didn’t plan to vote.

Hinojosa ‘s showdown in the Lone Star State come as Democrats look to make key gains in the midterms amid rocky political territory for the GOP. Some polls have placed Talarico, another Democratic state representative, ahead of Paxton for Texas’ open Senate seat — which a Republican has occupied for the past three decades.

In recent years, Texas Democrats have sought to notch statewide electoral wins but haven’t had much success, such as in the 2018 Senate race between former Rep. Beto O’Rourke (D) and incumbent Sen. Ted Cruz (R).

articles.title: After 'Lake America,' Trump suggests a new name for the state of New Mexico
articles.summary: The White House reposted Trump's Truth Social image showing New Mexico crossed out and rebranded as "America" days after the Lake America order.
articles.body: The White House on Sunday amplified President Donald Trump's call to rebrand New Mexico as "New America," reposting an image from the president's Truth Social account showing the state's name crossed out and replaced with "America." Trump's original post featured a map of the Southwestern state with the word "Mexico" crossed out in bright red and replaced with "America," effectively depicting it as "New America." TRUMP RENAMES LAKE ONTARIO ‘LAKE AMERICA’ AMID INTENSIFYING US-CANADA TRADE DISPUTE The White House later shared the image on its verified X account. Neither post included an explanation or indicated whether it reflected an actual policy proposal. The post comes just days after Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario "Lake America" for U.S. federal use. The executive order followed a series of tariff disputes between Washington and Ottawa. Trump said he directed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and the department to update the Geographic Names Information System to reflect the name change. Google and Apple later updated their maps for U.S. users to reflect the change. MAJORITY OF AMERICANS REJECT TRUMP'S RENAMING OF LAKE ONTARIO TO 'LAKE AMERICA,' POLL FINDS Trump also signed an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America" early in his second term. Unlike lakes and other geographic features that can be renamed for federal use through executive action, a president cannot unilaterally rename a U.S. state. Trump and the White House have not announced any formal effort to change New Mexico's name. The name "New Mexico" predates the state by centuries. Spanish explorers began using "Nuevo México" in the late 1500s. The territory kept the name after becoming part of the United States in 1848 and later achieved statehood on Jan. 6, 1912. articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: Congress set to protect AM radio and American discourse
articles.summary: WFMD in Frederick, Maryland, marks 90 years on AM radio as Congress prepares to vote on a bill requiring AM antennas in every new car sold.
articles.body: In 2026, the WFMD radio station in Frederick, Maryland, is celebrating its 90th year on the AM airwaves, and thanks to a bipartisan bill set for a vote in Congress this week, every new car sold in America will have an AM antenna to pick up its signal. The AM Radio For Every Vehicle Act already has more than 300 co-sponsors in the House, 60 in the Senate, and has been pitched mainly as a measure to ensure that emergency messages — the ones that start with the shrill whistle — can be sent out to cars through the AM stations. The commonsense measure is a good plan B to have in place in cases of cyberattacks or cyber outages, because sometimes the old ways can be the best ways. STEVE FORBES, STEPHEN MOORE: AMERICA MUST FREE ITS AIRWAVES BEFORE CHINA PULLS AHEAD That is a laudable goal, and by itself enough to warrant the legislation. But in fact, this measure can do more than protect lives, it can protect civil American discourse. AM radio is one of the last vestiges of it we have left in this digital age. All across the country, there are little stations like WFMD, with a predictable schedule that starts with a light-hearted but local-news-heavy morning show, then late-morning to mid-afternoon nationally syndicated news shows, followed by an afternoon drive-time call-in show that covers local, state and federal politics. In Frederick, the local afternoon show, "Mid-Maryland Live," belongs to Tim May and Frank Mitchell: the former, a cantankerous conservative wordsmith with a Maryland twang, and the latter, the patient and pleasant liberal New York City transplant with the dulcet radio voice. FCC CHAIR SUGGESTS ABC SKIPPING TRUMP'S SPEECH WILL FACTOR IN LICENSE RENEWAL DECISION The discourse that Tim and Frank engage in for three hours a day, along with the callers — many of whom are longtime regulars — is arguably the most balanced view of what is happening in the world that one could ask for, and almost always free from yelling and vitriol. Local AM radio is also the most reliable way to know what matters to people in communities outside major cities. For example, while data centers are a relatively new issue in the macro news ecosystem, I have been hearing about it for well over a year on local AM stations all over the country. It was almost never inchoate rage or unvarnished praise over data centers, but rather a very nuanced conversation from listeners who understand the laws and regulations of their communities with almost encyclopedic knowledge. We live at a time when, perhaps rightfully, we bemoan the demise of so many local small town newspapers along with the coverage and accountability they used to provide. But in many ways, that slack has been picked up by AM radio, where appearances by local officials are extremely common. ABC HAS NO BUSINESS ON PUBLIC AIRWAVES BECAUSE IT OPERATES 'LIKE A PARTISAN CABLE NETWORK,’ WATCHDOG TELLS FCC These same stations are usually also the repository for high school sports, giving kids the chance to feel that their effort matters when their exploits are broadcast live to the community. Some small government types might object to the government handing local AM radio stations this boon of enforcing access to their product, but it is a much more sensible way to help the radio industry than the National Public Radio model of direct funding. We have all seen that, for a myriad of reasons, publicly funded radio — absent the constraints of the free market — always winds up extremely far left. But local AM radio keeps the lights on by selling ads, usually to local businesses, and has a financial incentive to create a broad, cross-aisle appeal. For those who think radio is a dying form, think again. Estimates suggest that 80-90% of Americans listen to AM or FM radio weekly, with more than 80% of car owners flipping it on when they fire up the engine. No, AM radio is not heading to the dustbin of history. Not now, and not anytime soon. Just as our parents and grandparents did, we tune in to get the weather or the traffic, or just to find out what is going on. Not in New York, not in D.C., but where we live. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The fact that our Congress, which would struggle to pass "Go" in Monopoly, is set to pass the AM Radio For Every Vehicle Act is a testament to the enduring power of our local radio stations, and a good sign that listeners in Frederick will have Tim and Frank to listen to for a long, long time.

articles.title: GOP Sen. John Kennedy hedges on support for Hegseth
articles.summary: Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) on Sunday dodged questions about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as other Republicans voice concerns over the Iran war and senior Defense staff turnover. NBC News’s Kristen Welker asked the senator on “Meet the Press” if he still had confidence in Hegseth. “Well, it’s not my place to have confidence in him,”…
articles.body:
Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) on Sunday dodged questions about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as other Republicans voice concerns over the Iran war and senior Defense staff turnover.

NBC News’s Kristen Welker asked the senator on “Meet the Press” if he still had confidence in Hegseth.

“Well, it’s not my place to have confidence in him,” Kennedy responded.

Welker pressed Kennedy, suggesting that as a senator, he should have an opinion on Hegseth’s leadership. The Louisiana Republican conceded, saying it was “clear” the Defense secretary has consolidated his power by firing “some pretty good people.”

“Whether they deserve it or not, I don’t know,” the lawmaker said. “I voted for him. I’d probably vote for him again until evidence is shown to me that he shouldn’t have fired these guys. But I’m not worried about the personalities.”

Kennedy said he was worried about two things, the first being that the U.S. needs “more butts, not just for Iran, but for the world.”

“And No. 2, we need to be partnering up with Ukraine to develop a new way to fight wars,” he added. “And that begins with drones. And No. 3, we need to give the military some more money.”

Kennedy noted that Congress would likely have to pass legislation in order to give more money to the Pentagon, something he anticipated Democrats would oppose.

The Defense Department recently came under fire by the House Appropriations Committee’s top Democrat for secretly attempting to divert billions in National Institutes of Health funding to bolster its own budget without congressional approval.

“And that’s the way I see it,” Kennedy said Sunday. “You may disagree, but that’s what makes the world go around.”

Senate Republicans will expect Hegseth to answer for the departures of several senior military officials, including Army Secretary Dan Driscoll — who resigned last week.

Hegseth and the Trump administration are also set to ask senators for more than $70 billion in emergency national security spending to cover the growing costs of the Iran war.

Lawmakers like Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), formerly of the Senate Armed Services Committee, have voiced frustration with Hegseth’s leadership, calling it “inept management.” Tillis also urged President Trump to fire the Defense secretary and “find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it.”

Senior Senate Armed Services Committee member Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said he was “disappointed” about Driscoll’s resignation. House Armed Services Committee Chair Mike Rogers (R-Ala.) said he was “tired of all the churn” within the Pentagon and called for “stability” in its senior ranks.

Hegseth is reportedly eyeing several Driscoll replacements — including Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell, assistant secretary of the Army Marc Andersen, assistant secretary of Defense Derrick Anderson and Rep. Brian Mast (R-Fla.), chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and an Army veteran.

articles.title: Trump administration expands mass deportations with noncriminals
articles.summary: A surge in immigration arrests is sweeping up immigrants with no criminal record whatsoever, including many who were already known by the government, as officers push to meet quotas set by the Trump administration. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers broke records for the second Trump administration with back-to-back months of arrests topping 50,000…
articles.body:
A surge in immigration arrests is sweeping up immigrants with no criminal record whatsoever, including many who were already known by the government, as officers push to meet quotas set by the Trump administration.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers broke records for the second Trump administration with back-to-back months of arrests topping 50,000 in July and August.

But the data undercut a long-running claim by the Trump administration that it is targeting the “worst of the worst” by removing those with criminal records.

In fact, more than half of those arrested — 55 percent — had no interaction with law enforcement whatsoever, while another 24 percent have faced charges but were never convicted, according to data obtained by the Deportation Data Project.

These statistics have raised reservations among some Republicans in Congress.

“I’ve been telling the administration that do not conflate the gangster with the gardener, the nanny with the narco,” said Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.), who represents a district where more than half the population is foreign born.

It’s a figure that reflects a growing dynamic in immigration enforcement under the Trump administration — going after those with pending asylum claims or are otherwise seeking to adjust their status who are already known to authorities.

“What this shows is that the Trump administration is expanding its mass deportation operations away from people who are public safety threats or who have had some interaction with the criminal justice system and towards everybody else in an effort to hit the quotas put on them by the White House,” Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow with the American Immigration Council, told The Hill.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has offered mixed messaging on the extent it is still prioritizing criminals for removal.

On social platform X, the department maintains that 70 percent of those arrested by ICE have criminal records — a statement that is demonstrably false based on its own data.

“I mean the 70 percent figure has not been true since May of 2025,” Reichlin-Melnick said.

“DHS has been giving the 70 percent figure for at least a year now. It’s not true. It hasn’t been true. The agency has released extensive data confirming that it’s not true.”

But in media appearances, leaders have also distanced themselves from stressing the importance of arresting criminals, even as media releases from the agency continue to tout deportations of “the worst of the worst.”

“These individuals that we’re going after — I don’t care if you have a criminal background or don’t have a criminal background, you chose to break the law when you came across our border illegally. It’s our position and our job to hunt you down and send you back to where you came from,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said this past week during an appearance on “The Ingraham Angle.”

Border czar Tom Homan also contradicted the DHS’s claims during an appearance on the same show in July.

“Just over half of everybody we’re arresting is a criminal. So about half are noncriminals,” he said.

“But bottom line is, everybody’s on the table. The numbers show it’s about half and half now. … And with the additional resources we got from the reconciliation bill, you wait to see what the numbers are this year.”

There have been several factors behind the uptick in arrests, from a stealthier approach to enforcement under Mullin that departed from the widely publicized raids used previously to more recent tactics like arrests of immigrants at airports.

“This is from all the different tactics coming together really for the first time. The street arrests happening at the same time you have all the check-ins for people, immigration court interactions. All that stuff’s coming together — the airport arrests,” said David Bier, director of immigration studies at the libertarian Cato Institute.

Bier noted that Mullin got to the department as “all these resources [were] coming online at the same time.”

“They’re paying people a huge amount of overtime. They have no worries about money, so you know that’s a big part of it too is they just have people working like crazy to get these through,” he said.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal (Wash.), the top Democrat on the House Judiciary subcommittee on immigration, said the less overt operations carried out by Mullin are in part due to the backlash to the much publicized raids carried out under former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.

“They are continuing this strategy quietly now because it was unpopular when it was loud. But they’re going to find out in November that it’s unpopular when it’s quiet as well,” she told The Hill.

“They’re just arresting anyone. It’s just all about their ultimate number.”

Reichlin-Melnick noted that many of those being arrested, beyond having no criminal record, are also people who are already in immigration processing.

“We’re seeing this expanded to people at airports, people who overstayed their visa solely because the U.S. government didn’t get around to adjudicating their case in time, and these are people who really have done nothing wrong. They took the path that the Trump administration itself used to say was the right way,” he said.

“More and more of those people are now being swept into the mass deportation machine, despite the fact that they have pending applications with the U.S. government and have been complying with every obligation put on them. So why is the administration going after them? Because in some ways they are the easiest targets. They tell the government who they are or where they live. … And so when the U.S. government needs to ramp up arrest numbers, it can just go after those people rather than having to find people that it doesn’t know about already.”

Bier noted the increase in the number of those arrested without a final order of removal — an order given by an immigration judge after determining someone should be deported — leaving them waiting in detention as they continue to fight their case.

“Pretty soon, it’s going to be a majority of their deportations are not going to be based on a final order of removal, which will be just a real threshold for proving the success of the strategy, which is arrest and detain people without removal orders, and then just hope they give up,” he said.

The surge in arrests has led to some backlash, even in solidly red Florida, where immigrant communities include naturalized citizens as well as those who do not have status.

“Look, I’ve always supported TPS for Venezuelans, for Haitians,” said Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart (R-Fla.), referencing the temporary protected status program that protects people who are otherwise deportable from being sent back to countries that are considered dangerous.

“Securing the border had to happen. It’s worked. It’s good. It’s good for our security. But some of the enforcement, I think, has been a bit of an overreach, to say the least — to say the least. I’ve expressed that.”

“You can enforce the border, but I think you also have to hopefully look at all the circumstances when you have some specific cases,” he added.

Salazar, who has sponsored the Dignity Act as a way to help those without legal status gain a pathway to remain in the country, said the administration has failed to account for the economic contribution made by those without criminal records who have been working in the U.S. for years.

“The people who’ve been here for decades in construction, hospitality, agricultural, healthcare, manufacturing [industries] — those people are needed, and we need it for the economy. It’s just that there is a disconnect. … The White House is not understanding that those people are needed for the economy,” she said.

“And that those are our values as Americans.”

articles.title: Top House Republican backs Max Miller: ‘I support anybody with an R by their name’
articles.summary: Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Mich.), the chair of the House Republican Conference, said Sunday she backs Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio), despite two of his former partners accusing him of abuse. “Listen, divorces are ugly. And I’m glad I’m not … in his shoes right now,” McClain told host Margaret Brennan on CBS News’s “Face the Nation.”…
articles.body:
Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Mich.), the chair of the House Republican Conference, said Sunday she backs Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio), despite two of his former partners accusing him of abuse.

“Listen, divorces are ugly. And I’m glad I’m not … in his shoes right now,” McClain told host Margaret Brennan on CBS News’s “ Face the Nation .”

The No. 3 House Republican added, “I support anybody with an ‘R’ behind their name. I hope when all of this comes out that it’s not true. But at the end of the day, we’ve got to let the process play out.”

Miller has kept his reelection campaign going, despite multiple GOP lawmakers calling on him to drop out after his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, accused him of abuse during custody proceedings.

Moreno, the daughter of Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno (R), said Miller threw hot water at her, held a gun to her head and broke their daughter’s collarbone. The two divorced last year and are battling for custody of the 2-year-old child.

Miller has denied the allegations , sued his ex-wife for defamation in May and filed paperwork for the House Ethics Committee to open a probe into him in August. His former father-in-law, Bernie Moreno, is among those calling on the lawmaker to resign.

Miller’s ex-girlfriend, former White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham, has also accused him of abuse. The congressman has denied that allegation.

But Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) backed Miller earlier this week, saying the Ohio Republican “has been a great member of Congress” since entering the lower chamber in 2023.

“He has some issues in his personal life he’s working through. The House Ethics Committee is looking into that and any implications it may have,” Johnson told CNN’s Manu Raju.

McClain took a similar approach, backing Miller in his race against Democrat Brian Poindexter. The Michigan Republican said Sunday she is focused on “keeping the House” in Republican hands, and praised Miller as a “good advocate for his constituents.”

She told Brennan, “He’s chosen to stay in the race. … I hope this comes out that he is OK. But at the end of the day, he’s our nominee right now. I wish the allegations … aren’t true.

“But at the end of the day, we’ve got to continue to do what’s right for the American people. And that’s what we’re trying to do, keeping more money in your pocket, making sure we secure the border and making sure crime rates are down.”

articles.title: Hasan Piker brushes off Dems who see him as a liability, names his '28 choice
articles.summary: Hasan Piker told Fox News his job isn't to help the Democratic Party, even as consultant James Carville called him "an idiot" who isn't a Democrat.
articles.body: Hasan Piker hears the growing chorus of Democrats condemning him for incendiary statements, and he has a message for the party: "My job is not to make the Democratic Party look good." The far-left Twitch streamer has boosted socialist candidates even as he created headaches for the broader Democratic Party in a midterm election cycle where it hopes to make major gains. The 35-year-old Piker — whose polarizing stances range from defending communist Chinese dictator Mao Zedong to comparing Zionism to "Nazism" — is a darling of the Democratic Socialists of America, but a potential liability for mainstream Democrats as November approaches. Piker said Democratic Party officials have not reached out to coordinate a strategy. "I have not had a conversation with anyone from the DNC," Piker said. "That would be very funny." JAMES CARVILLE DECRIES 'IDIOT' HASAN PIKER, ORDERS DSA TO CHANGE ITS NAME In an exclusive interview at the 2026 Socialism Conference in Chicago, Piker told Fox News that, while he tries "to be as careful as possible" when it comes to choosing his words, his hours-long streams present his opponents with the "perfect opportunity to create viral media moments." Some of those moments include intense backlash over Piker’s 2019 statement that America "deserved 9/11," a comment which has been widely condemned by politicians on both sides of the aisle. HASAN PIKER CALLS REPUBLICAN PARTY THE 'BIGGEST DOMESTIC TERRORIST' IN THE COUNTRY Piker acknowledged that he should not have used the word "deserved," but said his point was that "[America’s] meddling in the affairs in the Middle East actually transpired these horrifying events." "It's not a controversial thing [to argue]," Piker said. "It was the language that I used that was controversial." HASAN PIKER CALLS HAMAS 'FAR MORE MODERATE,' DISMISSES TERROR GROUP’S BRUTAL RULE IN GAZA Piker's brash commentary gives him credence with the far-left DSA, which pulled off a host of primary victories against more moderate Democrats, but party elders have disavowed him. "There’s two things that I know about Hasan Piker," longtime Democratic Party consultant James Carville told Fox News Channel last week. "One, he’s an idiot, and two, he’s not a Democrat. So, I don’t answer for idiots, and I don’t answer for people who are not Democrats." VAN JONES WARNS FAR-LEFT SOCIALIST AGENDA IS 'REGRESSIVE' THREAT TO DEMOCRATIC PARTY Key Democrat lawmakers, including House Minority Leader Hakeen Jeffries, senators Cory Booker, D-N.J., and Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., and several House members have condemned Piker's past rhetoric. As he crosses the country, joining campaign rallies and canvass launches for liberal challengers to establishment-backed candidates, Piker acknowledged that even his allies have urged him to moderate his rhetoric for the sake of their electoral chances. DEMOCRATS' CIVIL WAR HEADS TO MICHIGAN WHERE PROGRESSIVES FACE BIGGEST TEST YET IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE SHOWDOWN But Piker told Fox News the press is overstating his association with the progressive political candidates and wondered why the media had not "demanded condemnations from establishment Republicans for collaborating with Charlie Kirk or using him as a campaign surrogate." Piker campaigned hard for Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive Michigan Democratic Senate nominee who pulled off a major upset victory against the establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens, D- Mich., in August. While his active support for El-Sayed may have generated buzz among Piker's base, it's also led El-Sayed to face a barrage of questions and criticism about his association with Piker. GRETCHEN WHITMER ENDORSES MODERATE HALEY STEVENS IN TIGHT UPCOMING SENATE PRIMARY Piker said that while he is confident El-Sayed – who distanced himself from Piker in recent weeks – will win this fall, "if people want to blame me" in the event El-Sayed loses, "they can blame me," adding, "I think that's the goal." Piker's role in the midterms may prove to be a warmup for the 2028 presidential election, and he said he has no plans to moderate his stances or stay on the sidelines. He said he will back socialist Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. if she launches a bid for the Democratic Party's presidential nomination. WATCH: AOC WON'T RULE OUT WHITE HOUSE BID AFTER POLL NAMES HER DEMOCRATS' TOP 2028 PICK "I think she's great," Piker said. "She would have some difficulties, of course, but hurdles can be climbed over, and I think she can do it." Piker believes his influence will continue to grow, and predicted even Democrats now condemning him will "try to utilize the platform that I have" if they seek higher office in 2028. 2028 BATTLEGROUND POLL SCRAMBLES DEMOCRATS’ FUTURE AS INSURGENT SOCIALIST SEIZES LEAD CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "And I'm not talking about my ideological allies or people who are associated with me right now," he added.

articles.title: Trump says White House helipad work is done after August project restart
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday announced that the White House helipad, which was redone at his request last month, has been completed. Trump posted a photo of former President Dwight D. Eisenhower on the White House lawn before departing in an Air Force H-13J helicopter in July 1957, becoming the first U.S. president to fly in…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday announced that the White House helipad, which was redone at his request last month, has been completed.

Trump posted a photo of former President Dwight D. Eisenhower on the White House lawn before departing in an Air Force H-13J helicopter in July 1957, becoming the first U.S. president to fly in a helicopter, on Truth Social. Eisenhower was leaving for Camp David, taking a helicopter at the insistence of the Secret Service, according to the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum .

“Dwight Eisenhower didn’t need a Helipad at the White House for those little Choppers, but America needs one now — Just completed, and MAGNIFICENT!” Trump wrote in the post.

The project began after crews removed the fighting arena from the White House’s South Lawn after the “Freedom 250 UFC” event to celebrate Trump’s 80th birthday in June. Trump said the following month that Sikorsky Aircraft, a subsidiary of Lockheed Martin and the company that manufactures the new helicopters for the president, is covering the $6 million cost of the project.

It was in August that Trump requested changes to the helipad. The Washington Post reported that Trump was dissatisfied with the construction. He showed interest in a landing pad level with the horizon and considered leveling the South Lawn’s slopes.

It is unclear what additional costs the new construction could add to the project.

Trump later showed the construction to reporters, praising the work on the helipad and the White House ballroom. He heralded how the helipad looked “incredible from the air and from every place else,” and emphasized how well it will look for future meetings with world leaders. He also signed the slab during his uninterrupted 30-minute tour with reporters.

The helipad is designed for Marine One, designed to be 100 feet wide and made from 4-inch-thick granite from a quary in California, with the helipad adorned with the presidential seal.

Workers told the president at the time that construction will be finished by Sept. 21, two days before Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to meet with Trump.

“We might make it for President Xi,” Trump said. “That’d be nice but not imperative.”

The helipad, along with the ballroom, is among several of Trump’s renovation projects across the nation’s capital.

Construction of the ballroom and the demolition of the East Wing received a wave of criticism from past administration officials and relatives of former presidents. It has also faced legal challenges, with the Supreme Court, in a split 5-4 decision last week , lifted a lower court’s block on construction.

The case raised by preservationists could return to the high court, but the ruling allows construction, made up from a 250-person crew working 20 hours a day, seven days a week, to continue.

articles.title: Armed person confronts Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton at event, campaign says
articles.summary: Acton was visiting the annual Canfield Fair in Mahoning County, near Youngstown.
articles.body: An armed person “lunged” at Amy Acton, Ohio’s Democratic nominee for governor, and injured several people at a fair, a campaign spokesperson said Sunday. Acton and her husband, Eric, “are grateful for the swift and decisive action of law enforcement and are praying for the recovery of those injured,” said the spokesperson, Addie Bullock. “This kind of violence has no place in Ohio,” Bullock added. “Dr. Acton will always stand up to the chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against one another.” The incident occurred Sunday afternoon while Acton visited the annual Canfield Fair in Mahoning County, near Youngstown. Acton, a physician, was not hurt, and remained on site to attend to one of the people injured, according to a photo an attendee shared with NBC News. The extent of injuries to others was not immediately known. Canfield police did not have immediate information about the incident or a suspect when reached by NBC News. The Ohio State Highway Patrol did not immediately respond to a request for information. Christopher Anderson, chair of the Mahoning County Democratic Party, said the incident happened while Acton was at the county party’s tent. “What happened at our tent today during today’s visit from Dr. Acton is reprehensible and should be condemned by leaders on all sides of the aisle,” Anderson wrote on Facebook. “MCDP is grateful for the quick response by our local law enforcement officials as well as the Ohio State Highway Patrol providing Dr. Acton security.” Acton was Ohio’s health director under term-limited Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican, in the early days of the Covid pandemic. She faces Republican nominee Vivek Ramaswamy, a businessman who ran for president in 2024, in the November general election to determine DeWine’s successor. Polls have indicated a close race. Ramaswamy also had been scheduled to visit the fair Sunday afternoon. “Candidates should be able to meet with voters without having to worry about threats or violence,” Ramaswamy spokesperson Connie Luck said in an emailed statement. “What happened today is completely unacceptable and has no place in politics, and we hope ... that no one was hurt.”
